speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some days ago the Leader of the Opposition asked whether I might say a word or two with regard to the meeting that took place last week with the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. I say to him at once that I undertook to do so the next day, but in the course of the debate that arose I omitted to do so.
The discussions I had with Mr. Macmillan provided an opportunity to renew at first hand the understanding of our respective points of view. As both the late Mr. King and former prime minister Mr. St. Laurent said on more than one occasion, such consultations are a feature of the unique quality of the commonwealth. It is one of the privileges of membership in this commonwealth that prime ministers who share these ties can hold friendly and forthright discussions with each other from time to time about the problems which affect their respective countries, and also in a broader world context.
In the talks we reviewed a number of international problems, ranging from the proposed summit conference to developments in the Middle East and the problems at the moment being faced by the republic of France. We also spent some time in exchanging views on economic developments, particularly those relating to the forthcoming commonwealth trade and economic conference.
As hon. members know, the Canadian government has felt that a summit conference might resolve some of the issues affecting relations of the free world and the communist bloc. But we also believe that before any such conference is called there must be full preparation on the lower levels in order to assure a reasonable degree of success. Many there are who look with anticipation to the holding of a summit conference as though it would resolve all of the problems, 57071-3-93
or many of the problems, that have existed between the free world and the communist countries since 1945. For that reason everything must be done, if a conference is to be called, to assure that it shall not fail in its objectives when it is convened. This would, I think, be worse than not having a conference at all.
As hon. members know, technical discussions will commence at Geneva on July 1 regarding atomic inspection and the detection of nuclear explosions, in which conference the United Kingdom, the United States and the U.S.S.R. will participate, as well as other interested countries. If in consequence of this meeting in Geneva tangible progress is made, I think we might then be more optimistic about a summit conference taking place. Mr. Macmillan and I hope that a summit conference will take place, but both are aware of the fact that the west has not yet had any very encouraging indications from the U.S.S.R. that would lead the free world to believe confidently that the cold war will cease. When I make that statement I do so as well in the light of events that have taken place in the last few days in Hungary, and also the extent to which Mr. Khrushchev has added to the propaganda warfare that has existed for the last year or so, and to an intensified extent in the last few days.
Reference was also made to the political developments in Lebanon, and recently my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs reported on the part Canada could take in co-operation with other members of the United Nations in assisting the security council in its efforts to bring about an end to the disorders in that country. It was agreed among us that respect for the ideals of the United Nations in the Middle East, as elsewhere, would be a help to the observers of the United Nations in their task in that area.
Another political development in the Middle East which has disturbed the free world, and particularly us in Canada because of our membership in the commonwealth and in NATO, has been the disorderly situation in Cyprus. I can only say that as a result of the initiative being taken by the United Kingdom government in its latest proposals that were revealed yesterday in the House of Commons there it is to be hoped that a solution of this
1458	HOUSE OF
Discussion with U.K. Prime Minister problem may be worked out within a framework of conciliation and compromise.
Discussions also centred around the situation in France, our close friend and valiant ally, and I think there is reason to be optimistic that the worst of the difficulties in that nation is over and that under General de Gaulle, our loyal and brave friend during the dark days of the last war, Canada will be able to look forward to seeing France resolve its present problems and to a continuation of intimate collaboration with France under General de Gaulle.
As well we discussed the economic outlook on both sides of the Atlantic and its relation to the main problems and issues of policy that the United Kingdom and Canada are now considering. These discussions involved trade and economic development, not only as regards our two countries directly but also in respect of our relations with other countries as well. The main subjects of economic discussion were the policies to be followed at and the preparations being made for the commonwealth trade and economic conference. This included a review of a number of matters that are being studied by officials from all commonwealth countries in London at the present time, to the end that proper foundations will be laid for a successful conference.
Throughout these discussions there was a full realization of the ever-growing Soviet attack on the vulnerable and comparatively weakly defended economic front of the free world. It seems clear that this economic challenge is designed to outflank the political and military defences of the west. I believe that counteraction will be required in this field and can only be taken by co-operative measures to meet this new Soviet offensive. During the next few months the Canadian government jointly with our friends and allies will take steps to meet this new Soviet offensive.
Discussions are already under way with the North Atlantic treaty council, and I believe the result we hope will be achieved at the forthcoming trade and economic conference in September will tend to strengthen the economies of the free world.
That in general represents in summation the matters that we considered and discussed.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word on the statement that has just been made by the Prime Minister. I think we have all welcomed the statement he has just made. We feel that having meetings from time to time between the Prime Minister of this country and the prime minister of any other commonwealth nation is an excellent thing and should be promoted. I was interested in his statement on the forthcoming commonwealth conference, but I felt the statement was somewhat vague and inexact and that it did not give us any great hope that real accomplishments might come from that conference. I am hoping that recent action taken by this government will not make the work of that conference more difficult.
We realize that throughout the world today there are many areas of great tension, and we hope the free nations of the world will have success in easing this tension and promoting freedom and democracy throughout the world. Along with the Prime Minister we in this group are concerned with recent events in Hungary, and we are afraid these may spell a change of tactics in the Soviet union itself. We hope also that the forthcoming conference in July on the control of atomic explosions and atomic inspection will prove fruitful.
As to the summit conference, we hope without reservation that one will be held, and held soon. I am not one of those who feel we should give undue weight to preparations being made in every single detail as a prerequisite to such a conference being held. We feel the west should seize the initiative now by agreeing readily to such a summit conference and, if it is a failure, allot the blame where it is due. But we could err by insisting there should be too much in the way of detailed advance preparation, thereby laying ourselves open to the accusation that we were making it more difficult for such a conference to be held. We hope such a conference will be held, that it will reduce world tension, and that it will result in the strengthening of freedom and democracy throughout the world.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I thank both hon. gentlemen for their contributions. I want to say,

in so far as the latter remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia are concerned, that all of us are desirous of having a summit meeting, but that a meeting called without adequate preparation would inevitably lead to unsuccess. This government has strongly supported the need for action with regard to a summit conference being called, but after all it is of prime importance that everything should be done in anticipation to assure that the issues will be properly placed before that conference, and the necessary preparations made for this purpose, so there will be no excuse for failure.
As far as the question asked by the Leader of the Opposition with regard to trade policy is concerned, we did discuss United Kingdom negotiations with the various European countries in the European free trade area, but there was no discussion of the United Kingdom plan for forming a free trade area with Canada.
Mention was made, I think the other day, with respect to the plans for the commonwealth conference. An agenda is being worked out; consideration is now being given to all the phases of the matters which should and will be discussed. As I said a moment ago, a meeting is now being held in London among the nations affected, to the end that the conference will have beneficial results.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF BASE PRICES FOR ONTARIO WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY
speechtext:
I wish to announce that, in accordance with the requirements of the Agricultural Stabilization Act, the agricultural stabilization board has established base prices, based on the average prices for the last ten years, for wheat, oats and barley.
The Ontario basis is as follows: Ontario wheat, $1.77 per bushel on track for No. 2 C.E. or better quality; Ontario oats, 72 cents per bushel on track for No. 2 C.E. or better quality; Ontario barley, $1.04 per bushel on track for No. 2 C.E. or better quality.
Using the above mentioned base prices the board has established a mandatory 80 per cent support price which will be in effect for the 12-month period starting July 1, 1958, as follows: Ontario wheat, $1.42 per bushel on track for No. 2 C.E. or better quality; Ontario oats, 58 cents per bushel on track for No. 2 C.E. or better quality; Ontario barley, 83 cents per bushel on track for No. 2 C.E. or better quality.
In the case of other provinces, outside the designated Canadian wheat board areas, where any of these grains are grown in commercial quantities, the support prices will be established in appropriate relationship to the above mentioned Ontario prices.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF BASE PRICES FOR ONTARIO WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY
speechtext:
With regard to the mandatory price of $1.42, am I not correct in saying that this is not the figure which has been urged upon the minister by a number of representative groups of Ontario farmers, who have discussed this matter with him within the last few months? Is it not also a fact that they have indicated the great danger in the future of a price at this level

Inquiries of the Ministry being construed as and developing into a ceiling price rather than a floor price?

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF BASE PRICES FOR ONTARIO WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY
speechtext:
As I indicated to the hon. gentleman the other day in connection with soybeans, every group of producers naturally asks for a very high support price and the wheat producers through the Ontario wheat board did, of course, ask for a considerably higher price than the mandatory support price provided under the stabilization act.
As far as this price becoming a ceiling is concerned, I do not think that will be the case, and I certainly hope it will not. The Ontario wheat board, in addition to having this support price provided for them, have applied to us under the Agricultural Products Marketing Act for authority to collect an equalization fee, as it might be called, or to make a levy of up to 9 cents per bushel to provide them with working capital to be used for taking care of this crop, paying storage charges and looking after the general handling of it. Their object, and I think this is what has been needed more than anything else as far as the marketing of Ontario wheat is concerned, is to prevent all this wheat from coming on the market in the fall.
The hon. member for Essex East will perhaps remember that shortly after the harvest season last summer this wheat was down to $1.12 per bushel. This present action provides an absolute floor of $1.42 per bushel; and I think the Ontario wheat board, by the use of this 9 cents levy which we have authorized them to collect, will be able to handle the crop, to feed it out gradually during the year and, I hope, to secure a considerably higher price than the $1.42. That, of course, is their objective.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday night the Minister of Finance paid tribute to the blue news in the budget. I think I should like to pay a suitable tribute to the recordbreaking overtones of red that were in the annual financial accounts.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as I approach this task I want to say I noted, as probably did the minister, the correspondent Adelphi's comment in the Financial Post last week when he was referring to the Prime Minister of Great Britain in complimentary form. He said this:
-Only a fool likes criticism, only a fool resents it.
I, of course, have received in the past a fair amount of criticism from the minister when he was sitting on this side of the house. Before too much criticism, may I say that there are naturally some features in the minister's proposals that I think will receive fairly general endorsation, although not too many in this particular budget. I can think of his proposal with respect to a gift to a spouse of real property up to a limit of $10,000. I think of certain additions to the list of sales tax exemptions to municipalities. I commend the minister for his references to the amendment to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I appreciate that, coming from a mining area as I do. However, I would point out that the assistance still would be at least $5 million short of the maximum assistance provided in one of the years of the previous administration. I think perhaps I should commend him for taking the tax off cut flowers; probably it helped me to some extent this morning.
But on the whole I do not think anyone could better the present Minister of Finance,
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson good orator that he is, in driving home small talk with a sledgehammer. I think of his peroration and I think also of his remarks last December 6, when he was speaking to the estimates of his department. At that time, as recorded on page 2009 of Hansard for that date, he said:
-We trust that the committee will however recognize the boldness of the government's program and the extent to which it will contribute to confidence and prosperity.
He was referring to tax reductions, Mr. Speaker, from that date to the end of the fiscal year, some five months, amounting to only $26 million. Again on Tuesday night in his speech to this house he referred to his "bold" budget. I refer to page 1250 of Hansard. The Minister of Finance said:
We have sought to face our difficulties squarely and to prescribe bold courses to meet them.
The tax reductions total only $8 million for the fiscal year. Mr. Speaker, I want to assert that in my view people are fast becoming disenchanted with rhetoric and thespian appeal only, and this dodge of too much government by bluff and by bragging.
I should like to refer to the deficit. This has received a considerable amount of attention in the press. I said on Tuesday night in my few remarks that I should like to say more about the prominent figure of $640 million produced by the minister after I had an opportunity to examine the complicated figures in Hansard. Out of office the Conservatives professed themselves in favour of less spending and balanced budgets. One can certainly argue for spending and deficits if they are not aimless but rather are planned, comprehensive and vigorous enough proposals to provide incentive, to provide lift, to perk up the economy. But I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that an analysis of this budget will show that the deficit is more attributable to political commitments than to economic theory or for the relief of unemployment.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How about
the old folks?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There was nothing in this budget with respect to the old folks. It results from piecemeal and unrelated measures. A deficit we can understand, but a deficit plus record unemployment shocks the country. The minister's financial leadership, now for almost a year, I suggest has solved neither deficit nor unemployment. He has added to both.
In so far as the gross national product is concerned, while the minister used a lot of words in his budget the other day he referred to it in a very passing way, and with what I felt was an inadequate build-up of
1464	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson the base to give confidence that the figure he finally produced is one upon which we can rely. It is quite possible to juggle accounts with respect to expenditures, as we saw the other night, but you cannot juggle accounts of revenues. "What will be", as the song goes, "will be."
The minister forecast revenues in 1958-59 of $4,660 million, down $387 million. Now, if this is to be realized the minister must be reasonably good as a prophet with respect to his estimate of gross national product, which he suggested on page 1235 of Hansard would be $32 billion.
I want to raise the question before the members of the house, is he a good prophet? First of all, has he made out any real case for his estimate? I want to compare his presentation, before tossing out this figure, with a similar presentation prior to a prediction of the gross national product made by his predecessor on March 14 of last year. I refer to Hansard pages 2216 and 2217 of March 14, 1957.
Before suggesting in any way what the gross national product might be the finance minister at that time referred to some of the components in the gross national product. He made reference to capital investment, and to the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, by his white paper, showed that capital investment was likely to increase by 7 per cent. Another component, namely commodity exports, according to Mr. Harris "should continue to increase through 1957." They did increase in 1957. Another component was consumer expenditures, and Mr. Harris said "these should continue to grow in 1957." He referred to the fact that a considerable increase in wage rates was built in through wage agreements recently made. Another component was farm income, and the minister of finance of that day said this should be maintained unless the grain crops in the west were disappointing. He referred to the labour force, and said he did not believe he "could count on as large an increase as in the previous year."
What in this budget have we had to establish the minister's estimate as a base for the gross national product? As reported at page 1235 of Hansard, blandly he said this:
-there are hopeful signs that we have reached the end of the recent decline.
With respect to investment intentions-I see nothing to justify a prediction of a rise in the gross national product-the minister said this:
Present investment intentions of business for capital outlays in 1958 are about 11 per cent below the 1957 level.


He went on to say that housing and governmental expenditures would be up perhaps 14 per cent, but I draw attention to the relative volume of investment in both accounts. Here we have, then, little to build up confidence that the gross national product estimate is something that we can rely upon. As reported at page 1235 of Hansard of last Tuesday the minister starts off by saying this:
Assuming-
And it is a big assumption.
-normal crops, stable prices and no untoward external events, I am basing my revenue forecasts on a gross national product of $32 billion, which is about 2 per cent above the level achieved in 1957.
As I say, he does that without giving us an explanation of the components of that very important figure. He says "assuming normal crops". We all hope that normal crops will prove to be the result in 1958, but already we are getting not too optimistic reports as to moisture conditions in the western provinces.
With respect to capital investment, we normally get from the minister of trade and commerce at this time a revised estimate of the white paper that we had to smoke out of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce in March, but which in its first page made clear that the calculations were based on information obtained at the end of 1957, in December of that year.
I wonder whether we are to expect in this debate the usual revised estimate of capital investment from the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I know that last week before a congressional committee in the United States a new figure was produced, and it by no means held up to the expectations produced at the beginning of this year respecting business capital investment plans.
In addition, I think some doubt is cast on the probability of the minister's forecast when we look at his own forecast of revenues for the coming year. I refer to page 1241 of Hansard of last Tuesday. He referred to personal income tax. He suggested that this tax would be down $129 million in the coming year. He referred to corporate income tax. He suggested that this tax would be down $215 million. He referred to sales tax. Sales tax, of course, would be related to consumer expenditures, a component of the gross national product. He suggested that this tax would rise, despite a population increase, by only 2 per cent for the coming year.
Another component of the gross national product, or having a very important effect upon it, would be exports. As the house knows, in the period January to April of this year exports are down $21 million. So

where out of any of these figures does one get comfort in thinking there will be a rise in the gross national product of 2 per cent, unless it comes-something which the minister discounted-from an increase in prices?
I suggest that the minister seems to have taken probably the most optimistic of all advice in calculating the gross national product. That leaves some doubt in the first instance, when we consider this matter of deficit, as to whether the revenue estimate of $4,660 million is attainable. But on the expenditure side we had this striking sentence in the minister's speech:
-we propose to eliminate the balance remaining in the national defence equipment account.
That amount was $165 million. That is an item to which a considerable portion of the press did not give very much prominence. This fund was set up by the predecessors of the minister in order to help NATO. I suggest that this is an item that is being raided at the present time in a bookkeeping manner to help the Conservative party. In looking at this budget in ensuing days I suggest that we confine ourselves to current operations. This particular kind of calculation is just about the equivalent of the minister saying, "Well, in days past my predecessors Mr. Harris and Mr. Abbott had surpluses; we will use them". That is just about what the result is when you take advantage of this $165 million in this particular account.

speechtext:
In addition there is a very interesting thing that I think could be said. I thought the minister was very casual in his arithmetic the other night. On careful reading we find that he produced a figure which established that in the main estimates we had $5,179 million; in the supplementaries, $58 million; in the hospital insurance act provision, $70 million; and for old age security deficit, $190 million. These add up to $5,497 million. He made reference to the possibility of a deficit on the Canadian National Railways, but he did not put it in his accounts. We already have the budget proposed for this year by the Canadian National Railways. The railroad itself suggests that its deficit in the coming year will be $55 million. Why leave it out? Adding this amount to the $5,497 million we come to $5,552 million, versus revenue of $4,660 million.
To me that provides a deficit of $892 million. Even if one takes the $5,497 million and even assuming there was any justification for the minister utilizing this $165 million as a transfer item and relating that to his
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson proposed revenue of $4,660 million, I suggest that he was rather casual indeed in ending up with the round figure of $5,300 million, because there is a difference of $32 million in that arithmetic, as I see it. But the minister may say "What's $32 million?"

speechtext: No, no; he does not.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He had some other items without any price tags. He said that we must expect some payments under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. That remains with a question mark. In addition he said there would be further "statutory requirements," whatever that means. Again there is no price tag. He said as well that the house can expect the usual final supplementary estimates. I think this will be in the minds of hon. members when they consider the deficit figure that was presented to the house and the country.
This presents, I admit, quite a guessing game to any person who is now examining these accounts. As I pointed out the other night, there is nothing here to suggest that the friend of the government, Mr. Frost, can expect his $78 million which, if he were to obtain, it would mean that an additional $150 million would have to go to the other provinces on the basis of equalization.
Another interesting point is that no mention whatsoever was made in the budget with respect to civil servants' salaries. They are negotiating with the government, I understand, for a 12 per cent increase, but supposing the figure were 8 per cent the cost of that increase would be $100 million. There is nothing here about the oft-discussed pensions for superannuated civil servants. Even the new item, produced with a considerable flourish the other night-the additional subsidy of $2 2 million for gold mines-does not seem to have been provided for.
The other night the minister made much of the appropriateness of the timing of proposals presented by him as financial leader of the country within the last year. I suggest that, on the contrary, the failure to realize what was happening, months after he took office, has resulted in the failure to act. As far back as last November the Trades and Labour Congress of this country called for action; they predicted that during the winter 500,000 persons would be unemployed. The Prime Minister brushed off this estimate, suggesting that these people were alarmists. That prediction, as everybody knows, proved to be conservative. I say the minister was so busy charging other people with thinking us into a depression that he did not do all

The Budget

Mr. Benidickson he should have done, in conjunction with his budget advisers, to think us out of the depression.
There is no bold new program provided by this government. I think it is most evident that the thinking which has taken place in past months has been preoccupied with elections, past and forthcoming, and not with matters of economics. The minister would say the bad signs were not there, and we have heard some suggestion that the previous administration was unduly optimistic; but allow me to point out that in the papers presented to us the other day the minister himself confesses that he, fairly early, had information upon which I consider he should have, acted promptly. At page 1232 of Hansard for June 17, 1958, the minister said:
Some slow-down in economic activity was to be expected after the excessive pace of 1955 and 1956, a pace which was straining our resources of men and materials despite very large borrowing abroad.
What was there in the budget of 1957 which would have given good counsel to the minister? At page 2217 of Hansard for March 14 of that year Mr. Harris, who was then minister of finance, said:
All in all, I believe, there is a good possibility that the inflationary pressures which have been present throughout the past year may begin to moderate during the coming year.
He went on to say in a cautionary way that the increases in exports might not be as great as they had been, and again in that same speech he said:
1 do not believe we can count on obtaining as large an increase in the labour force.
At page 2217 again, in the 1957 budget report, Mr. Harris also said:
Corporate profit margins show signs of narrowing.
We have found that that was indeed a pretty good prophecy. The minister, however, boasted the other night of good timing. I suggest that during last fall and winter we in this country had very little except soothing words from the new ministers, particularly from those most identified with the recession, namely the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Labour, and indeed the Prime Minister himself. The Minister of Finance said on November 23, 1957, that there was no national emergency in unemployment. "The number of people employed in mid-October is the highest in Canada's history." He said if this was a national emergency all he could say was that practically every country in the world would like to have a national emergency like it.
I contrast that with what the minister said the other day in his budget papers, and I refer once more to page 1232 of Hansard for


June 17. In reporting upon the affairs of the country under his administration he said:
By mid-1957 the value of large capital projects being started began to run behind the value of projects being completed.
On the same page he said:
-during 1956 capital expenditure was rising at a rapid rate while in 1957 investment outlays as a whole first levelled out and then declined slightly. The slow-down in the rate of capital investment was accentuated by the inventory liquidation which developed toward the end of the year.
That is to say, toward the end of 1957. Again, with respect to unemployment, was the minister not aware of these things? At page 26 of the white paper provided to this house the day before the budget speech we find the following words:
There were more persons with jobs in each month of 1957 than in the corresponding period of 1956, but in the fourth quarter of the year the gains became progressively smaller as employment began to show the effects of the levelling out in production.
And at page 27 of the white paper we find the following words:
The low in unemployment occurred in June, 1957, when 162,000 persons were jobless, compared with 117,000 during the same period in 1956. From the third quarter to the end of 1957 unemployment just about doubled and there were 386,000 jobless persons in December compared with 186,000 a year earlier.
What was the Minister of Finance really saying to the country? This surely is indicative of his thinking at that time. On December 8, when speaking to the Dominion Commercial Travellers Association meeting, he is quoted as saying that "a decline in the volume of our imports is too fractional to be a cause of concern." On December 6 last, in presenting the estimates of his department to this house, he said he was still prepared to accept the estimates of revenue of his predecessor. The Minister of Labour, as late as March 8 last at a press conference in Vancouver, said, "We are over the peak."
With what did these words meet within a matter of a few days? The figure for unemployment produced by the dominion bureau of statistics showed there were 35,000 more unemployed people in the month of March than there were in February. Once again we hear soothing words from the Minister of Finance. The other night he said that hopeful signs are here, that "we have reached the end of the decline." There is no one in this house who does not hope the minister is correct; but the ministers I have quoted, the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Finance and indeed the Queen's first minister, have misread the economic signs so often in the past that there is some doubt cast upon the assertions now being made. I do not want to be a Jeremiah continually today, but we have to be realistic.

Another item which I think should get more attention than simply the absolute reduction in the number of unemployed is the rate of reduction. I find that registration at the unemployment commission's offices in the worst previous year of our post-war depression, which was 1955, went down between mid-March and mid-April from 633,000 to 556,000, which is a drop of 12 per cent. But this year at mid-April the figure was 884,000, down 30,000, it is true, but the rate of drop instead of being 12 per cent was 3 per cent.
I should like to say a few words now about trade, although during the forthcoming debate many others in this party will have something to say on this all-important subject. I referred to it briefly on Tuesday night. I spoke then of what I regarded as the seeming ham-handedness and the casting of a preconference chill over such things as the forthcoming commonwealth conference, particularly with respect to the proposed tariffs affecting British wool imports. I said that the same thing had been done, in my opinion rather ineptly, just prior to the Mont Trem-blant conference last year. It does not seem to me that actions of this kind are likely to be very encouraging to the delegates to this assembly. We also remember very recently how vigorously we all cheered-and none of us more than the government members of this house-the speech of the Prime Minister of Great Britain. If anything I think his visit to North America, stripped of economic jargon, was basically intended to suggest ways of making the capitalist system work in the cold war. He wanted to persuade us all that we needed some new economic thinking on the part of the west. This, I think, has bread and butter implications for Canada.
I think, again in relation to the budget the other night, of the forthcoming visit, not far off, of President Eisenhower. But despite this approaching visit, which is of great importance, the Minister of Finance unnecessarily, I think, took time out in the usual hot-headed way he has with respect to the United States to introduce this subject which was so much discussed during the recent political activities. To me this business of stirring up anti-United States sentiment played up as an election issue is not desirable. I refer to the remarks of the Minister of Finance as reported at page 1237 of Hansard.
What is the basis of all this? Can it be that it is largely personal pique? Time magazine of April 26, 1958, referred after the election to what it called the flying visit to Washington of the minister for external affairs and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and then the article said:
Since they were in town, the two ministers decided also to drop in on their two U.S. counterparts. Commerce Secretary Sinclair Weeks turned
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson out to be too busy to see Churchill in his office, but that evening the two managed to link arms at a cocktail party.
I have no critical reference to make to the latter part, but I wonder if it is pique that is responsible for continued affronts to a country which continues to be Canada's best customer. I think there is still rankling in the mind of the government this phrase, after their last attempt to do something constructive and important in this field, when so much emphasis was given to the phrase "we fixed 'em".
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if you were a businessman with one big customer and a number of smaller ones and you wanted to enlarge your business, you would try to be nice to all your customers; you would not tell your big customer, "I want to do business with more people, so I want to do less with you". That would be very unwise and I suggest not likely. The Gordon commission suggested in its report that in times of recession-and we have such times now-it would be found that our exports to the United States would hold up better than our exports overseas. This happened in 1957 and it is happening today. In 1957 our exports to the United Kingdom fell by $75 million, while our exports to the United States rose by $51 million.
I have no doubt we will have a further opportunity to consider what the government has in mind by its reference in the budget speech to dumping. We will have a statute and be able to examine the language of that statute and debate it in due course, so I do not propose to go into this subject to any great extent. The announcement of the change in the dumping laws will have to be examined in the light of the legislation when it is brought down, but on its face it appears to be another "back to Bennett" item repeating his very special kind of dumping laws which consumers in this country will remember. From what the minister has already said it appears that there is great danger that these dumping laws will be used as a weapon to harass producers in other countries rather than as a legitimate instrument of government economic policy.
One of our most serious and justified complaints against the Americans-and this was referred to in the minister's speech the other night-is that they use regulations of various kinds to keep out our exports. The minister's remarks with regard to this appear on page 1237 of Hansard. Today it looks as if, with this new weapon which the minister is adopting, we are in danger of doing exactly what so angers us when the United States do it; and we are doing it just prior to this

The Budget-Mr. Benidickson very important visit by the President of the United States and Mr. Dulles.
This is typical of some of the ineptness which has preceded conferences of the greatest importance to this country. We are not fooling anybody by this, particularly our best customers. The other day in Washington the United States ambassador to Canada, Mr. Merchant, appearing before the Senate foreign relations committee had this to say:
Mr. Diefenbaker can be expected to continue to protest eloquently and with vigour what he considers protectionist action by the United States, while at the same time yielding to protectionist pressure groups in Canada by imposing restrictions on certain categories of imports.
How is trade to be enlarged by this kind of procedure?
Now I should like to make reference to a subject which has been discussed several times this session, namely the public works program of this government. I said when speaking on the first interim supply bill that one can of course argue for spending and deficits in a recession. The government would like the people of Canada to believe that the new high expenditures and large deficit are due to deliberate planning and an unusually large public works program. With the present government's Madison Avenue technique to which we have become accustomed, I think they have been somewhat successful in attaining this objective. Articles in the press have certainly tended to foster this idea. A big play was made by the Prime Minister with the word "launch" when he spoke of the launching of a vast program of public works. Of course he linked with it a big program to combat unemployment.
Careful examination of the figures, as I have pointed out previously this session in the house, quickly reveals that the figures presented are largely normal spending by a government, expenditures that would be presented by any government. They are not new; they would be provided in good times or bad. In confirmation of that statement I wish to make reference to table 3 in a press statement presumably put out by the Minister of Finance on May 13, when he was releasing the main estimates in this house for the coming year. This table has been broken down into four headings:	"Administration
and operation", "Building, works and equipment", "Grants, subsidies and other items" and "Recoverable items". The total allotment for "Buildings, works and equipment" for the period 1958-59 is $927.3 million as compared with $923.5 million for the 1957-58 period provided by the previous administration in a time of economic inflation and with very little thought when under preparation


of the more difficult winter ahead in 1957-58. This indicates that on May 13, 1958, there was nothing very planned or striking in the public works proposals of the present government.
In addition I remind the minister that when he spoke on his estimates on December 6, 1957, he said very clearly that where there are expenditures that involve construction which means employment, items would not be reduced. I draw his attention to the fact that not long afterward he was called upon to approve a warrant to be presented to the Governor General for expenditures for the balance of the year. The warrant is dated February 15, 1958, and it discloses reductions in construction votes totalling almost $20 million. There is a reduction in construction votes of $11,501,636. From that must be deducted some increases in construction votes but they amount to only $66,576, leaving a net reduction of $11,435,060 in the ordinary accounts, plus reductions for construction in the loan accounts of $8,501,490 making a total of $19,936,550.
There is altogether too much rhetoric and not enough reality in some of the actions of this government, and as I have said the public will soon realize this. Too much of what we hear proves to be pretty empty, almost phony when it receives careful examination. I want to bring the house right up to date. If there is anything the government has done about which we have heard much in recent weeks it has been the steps it took with regard to the housing program. Reference to housing has predominated from the time of the speech from the throne on, and we have heard a great deal about the housing program of this government in terms of it being a work-creating measure.
After the speech from the throne was announced nothing received more attention from the press than the government's $350 million housing program. Indeed with typical flair and a typical sense of publicity value the throne speech debate itself was interrupted to permit the house to deal with amendments to the National Housing Act. It was said to be an emergency measure, and it was most important that the amendments be passed involving the expenditure of $350 million for housing which would make available work for the unemployed. Within a matter of a week or perhaps two weeks after this splashy and very well-huckstered window dressing we found that this proposal was just as empty as are so many other proposals that are well advertised; as empty as a bird's nest in December.
After the bill was passed by this house the subject of the government's housing

program could only command from the press and from the public the usual yawning. But the truth comes out. I want to read what the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation had to say with respect to this additional $350 million, when he appeared before the standing committee on finance of the other house on Thursday, June 5, 1958 as recorded at page 29 of the minutes of proceedings of that committee. Mr. Bates said:
-we are standing merely on residual loans ... It is my opinion . . . that by the end of the year, if we got into it again in September-
He was referring to direct lending.
-we might have spent $30 million or something of that kind-
-by the end of the year. What a contrast between rhetoric and deeds, promises and performance.
If there is anything in the new budget that probably had a chance of making an appeal to the average member of the public I think it was the reference to deducting for income tax purposes certain prescription drugs. Actually this again is a window dressing item, because in the budget brought in by Mr. Harris last year a standard deduction of $100 was provided to all taxpayers, and at that time on advice of the officials of the department the minister said that about 75 per cent of the taxpayers of the country had not put in claims of this kind and therefore it was a clear, new deduction.
I think the Minister of Finance has been found out on this, too. Just yesterday the Financial Post, a very authoritative and highly respected financial publication in this country, commented on the new budget in these words:
There is flashy political appeal in some of Finance Minister Fleming's tax changes, but when citizens get them digested and when they figure out what the changes could actually mean to them, there will be widespread disappointment.
Making drugs and medicines, eyeglasses and artificial eyes, ambulances and laboratory services exempt from income tax, will catch popular fancy.
But the 3 per cent of income limit on such income tax deductions, which Mr. Fleming retains, still means that very few people will be sick enough to get any benefit whatever from the change. If the Tories wanted to do anything significant on reducing this human burden, they should have lowered the 3 per cent figure so long recommended by tax experts and then the sick would have had an honest benefit.
The same thing applies to some of the other income tax changes announced. These gestures will look and sound good in the constituencies, but they will mean very little or nothing to all but a very few people-and very, very little of them.
I will have additional opportunities in the further stages provided in the budget debate to comment on some of the other items of the budget, but I want to repeat what I said on Tuesday evening; that contrary to what
The Budget-Mr. Argue the minister said then there is nothing in this budget which suggests bold courses. We have a deficit not by design but by default. There is nothing new in the budget either for jobs or for business. I therefore move the following amendment, seconded by my deskmate, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill):
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that the government, in its budget proposals, has failed to cope satisfactorily with the problems of the recession in spite of the largest peacetime deficit in Canadian history and that it is moving towards greater trade restrictions at a time when other countries in the western world are moving in the opposite direction."

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the wording of the amendment should recommend it to the house and to the country. Certainly our group is quite happy to support the amendment as it has been moved. I believe that by the time I draw to the conclusion of my remarks my colleagues, who are very good draftsmen, will be able to hand me a subamendment which will also commend itself to the country.
I congratulate the Minister of Finance on his facility in both languages and I say to him quite sincerely that I envy him in this regard. I was most interested in his budget speech. I can only say that I wish he had presented such a comprehensive budget statement in the last parliament a few months ago.
I also want to commend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) on his effort as financial critic for the official opposition. I enjoyed his remarks. In fact when there was a lot of punch in them I enjoyed them exceedingly. I congratulate him on the effort he made.
I think this budget will be taken by the people of Canada as something of a shock. One hears of shock treatment being used at times by the medical profession. I think the budget is shock treatment for the people of the country. It demonstrates that we on this side of the house were right when we said in the last parliament that the government owed it to the country to present a comprehensive budget that would hide nothing and would show the true financial picture of the nation. That was not done. There was no budget in the last parliament. There was no comprehensive statement as to what would happen in the ensuing fiscal year.
What did we have last session? When the government was criticized about economic conditions the main thing we had was the waving before the house of a so-called secret document that had been presented to the former government and not divulged by them. We had a motion in the house the other day
1470	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Argue asking that the up to date version oi the same secret document be now divulged, and the government would have nothing to do with it.
I think the document that should have been divulged before the election is the budget speech of the Minister of Finance. If that document, which was kept secret until after the election, had been available to the people of the country I have no doubt that the results of the election would have been a great deal different; because the government, by refusing to disclose the economic facts facing the nation, was able to camouflage the true position of the country and to benefit in a political sense. This is an ice water budget which I think will awaken the people of Canada to the fact that on March 31 they were cheated, as has been proven by the government's lack of action since that date.
I sat on this side of the house for many years with members of the present government, and I was just as energetic in criticism of the former government as I am now. I had expected until a very few weeks ago, as a matter of fact, that the government would continue for some time on the road it took last session, a road of progressive legislation, a road to improve the economic lot of the ordinary people of the country. But I have been fooled. They have now halted that forward progress. The Conservative party which goes by a hyphenated name-

speechtext:
He forecast a 2 per cent increase in the gross national product. The increase in the population of the country is ordinarily about that figure, so we are going to remain just where we are with widespread unemployment, with the agricultural industry in a state of depression and in many parts in almost total collapse, without any policy, without any action by the government to improve the economic position of the people of the country.


The Minister of Finance is a great master of words. He has shown us that he can champion either side of a cause with equal ease and facility.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And equal volume.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He has contradicted himself so often in the budget that it is a double-barreled budget with the barrels pointing in opposite directions. What did he say before he had completed one full page of his address as it appears in Hansard? As found on page 1231 of Hansard of June 17 he said:
Foremost among the factors which we must keep in mind in reviewing the year 1957 is the record population increase of 552,000, an increase which brought our population at year-end to 16.9 million. About half of this growth was the result of natural increase and about half was due to the exceptionally high level of immigration.
Some idea of the economic importance of this great increase can be gained from the fact that there are only three Canadian cities with a population in excess of half a million people.
Then he went on:
Population growth of itself does not ensure progress, but in a country such as ours it has a special significance. It provides a greater market for our agricultural produce and for the products of our factories and reduces our vulnerability to changes in external demand. It brings us a greater diversity of talent and the means of employing it to better advantage. It reduces the per capita cost of supplying essential services in this great land.
Here we have outlined all the advantages of an increase in population, half of which was brought about by natural increase and the other half from immigration, yet the government chokes off immigration as one of its first actions on taking office. They choked off immigration which, according to the words of the Minister of Finance, had done so much for the economic welfare of this country. We have double talk from the Minister of Finance.
During the last session we heard a great deal about the improvement that was to be made in the old age pension, the improvement in the position of people obtaining social security benefits. We welcomed the improvement. What were we told? We were told that the improvement for the old age pensioner was not the end but was only the beginning. The Prime Minister said he was having an inquiry made into the social security system in the United States, and he was in a hurry to have this inquiry made. He appointed Professor Gordon Huson and set out a tight timetable of three or four months for the work. The professor said it was not long enough, so he was promptly dropped and another man, Dr. Robert Clark of the University of British Columbia, was appointed. The aim was to get a report within

three or four months so that Canada would have the advantage of an improved social security system.
Well, the report has not yet been made, though it is more than four months since Professor Clark was appointed. More important, when I asked the Prime Minister on May 30 when a report would be received, and whether when it was received action would be taken this session to improve the old age pension, what did he say? He said, as reported at page 677 of Hansard for that date:
As to whether or not action will be taken at this session of parliament, I must say that having regard to the tremendous amount of work yet to be done as set out in the speech from the throne, I would not expect it would be possible to give consideration to the report, even if received now, to enable any legislation to be brought in at this session.
The people of Canada have been fooled and hoodwinked in this regard, because they expected an early report. They expected early action. Why should parliament not sit for another three or four days this session- let us assume it would be a long debate-to discuss and pass legislation providing for an improved system of social security? The reason there is no hurry now is not that there is so much legislation before the house, the reason is that the election is over. The urgency is over, and there is plenty of time to consider the matter during another session of parliament at some time in the future. I ask the Minister of Finance if he has anything to say as to when such action will be taken.
How much did we hear from the government before the election about the need to increase commonwealth trade? This was the big pitch of the Conservative party. They were going to increase commonwealth trade, and they were going to call a conference. They did call a conference, and they received an offer which they have not yet answered. It made them dizzy when they heard it, and they have not yet recovered sufficient equilibrium to provide a reply. We thought we were going to hear something about the government's plans for freer trade, but we did not hear anything in the budget last year. We thought there might be something in the budget this year. However, the budget contains the same old Tory policy all the way through of higher and higher tariffs, more and more obstruction to international trade. This policy is not going to help industries or the people who work in industries. I suggest it is directed toward helping some of the management; it may help a few of the owners. The report of the tariff board on the woollen industry says this policy will not save the industry.
If the government wanted to take action, instead of putting up the tariff why did
The Budget-Mr. Argue they not remove the excise tax on clothing? This would have increased the home market for woollens and other goods. Why not provide full employment, with the resultant tremendous increase in demand for textiles that would follow such a program? There has been no planning on trade. There is nothing in the budget except a reversion to the old Tory policy of higher and higher tariffs.
I thought last session that perhaps the new look of the Conservative party might stay. I thought perhaps the Prime Minister would use his influence, and would have sufficient influence in the cabinet, to break down trade barriers and to overcome the Tory members of the cabinet. He lost out if he did try, and I do not know whether or not he did. This provision in the budget for higher and higher tariffs has all the earmarks of being made on Bay street, or having been written in the board room of the Toronto stock exchange. Certainly the budget contains nothing for the ordinary people of this country.
I know the Minister of Finance took a long time to outline the various reductions in excise taxes, the increased exemption for medical expenses, the little here and the little there. However, there is not very much in total, only $8 million over a year as compared to the $26 million in the legislation brought in last year. I have a statement here, the source of which I shall give a little later on. It was made about similar reductions in a budget not so long ago. The statement is as follows:
It is an illusory budget. It proposes changes, large in number but small in individual extent in every case, and seeks to create the impression of importance by their mere multiplicity. The banquet table is long. It is well dressed. The best silver and china are used. The lackeys are well-trained. But the fare is thin. The guests have left unsatisfied.
This was a statement by the present Minister of Finance in this house on March 21, 1957, as recorded at page 2553 of Hansard. I believe that is a far more appropriate and more accurate description of this budget than I am able to give. This government, with its double talk, with its progressive face of last year and its Tory face of this year, is just as inconsistent in all its actions.
We heard a great deal about the government wanting to help education in this country by providing further grants to assist young people in obtaining an adequate education.
There is really nothing in this budget except to coax the corporations to do some of the things that the government itself could be doing by way of grants for education. The Minister of Finance had this to say as far
1472	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Argue as the application of income tax law is concerned, as reported at page 1244 of Hansard:
It is important that income tax law should receive constant attention to ensure the greatest degree of equity in its operation.
Yet the dividends from investments in corporations are still, to a very substantial extent, not taxable. We find that a married person can earn $11,350 without paying any income tax whatsoever with the exception of $60 old age security tax. Is there any equity amongst Canadian taxpayers with this provision still remaining in the budget? Have any steps been taken to tax into the federal treasury some of the enormous speculative profits that are being made in the gas pipe-line corporations of this country? How roundly the Conservatives criticized the Liberal government for their actions in connection with gas pipe lines. If we pick up almost any paper in recent days we find that Conservatives all over this country, whether they be high-placed Conservatives in Ontario or high-placed Conservatives with another name in the province of Quebec, have all got their elbows or their arms into this very lucrative deal, or as somebody says, their nose in the trough. They are still exempt. There is no capital gains tax. Yet the minister talks about equity in taxation.
Here is another instance where we find the government talking both ways. Before the election they said they were going to call another conference or reconvene the federal-provincial conference. That categorical statement was made by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Finance. But there is not a word about it in the budget, not a sound or a breath. Before the election the calling of a conference was announced. After the election no interest is shown in the conference.
The agricultural producers of this country expected fair treatment by this government. They put great stock in the Agricultural Stabilization Act passed in this house last year, and in the clause which said that floor prices would be established in relation to the cost of production taking into consideration the farmer's investment and a fair labour income. The farm organizations came down here a few weeks ago after the election and said to the government, "What are the cost of production figures?" The government said, "We do not have any; there are no statistics available". The legislation says the farmer is to have the cost of production, but the government are not trying to find out what the cost of production is.
As I said earlier in the session, the western producers expected that deficiency payments on grain would be made. To show their confidence that something would be done, after


the election was over they came to Ottawa and asked for deficiency payments of something in excess of $220 million in total on two crops of grain. But in the budget there is not a word about that, not a breath.
In calculating this huge deficit, no account has been taken of the possibility of deficiency payments on western grain for the last two crops. I say that at this moment this government has turned thumbs down on the farmers' request for deficiency payments. I say that the government has failed to fulfil that promise, and at this moment has no intention of fulfilling that promise; because if they had, the deficit forecast would have been much greater. The only hope for western producers at this time is to join their farm organizations in greater numbers and put a great deal more pressure on this government by way of submissions and by way of interviews.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF CANADIAN REPRESENTATIVE AT FORTHCOMING CONFERENCE ON NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reverting to motions at this time I would like to make an announcement concerning a matter of immediate importance respecting the projected talks on the technical methods of verifying compliance with an agreement on the suspension of nuclear tests.
Exchanges on this question have taken place in recent weeks between the United States and the Soviet union, the latest of which was in the form of a letter dated June 13 last from the Soviet union, to which the United States has delivered its reply as of today's date.
Hon. members will understand that it is not for me to make public the text of this communication, which will be released in accordance with procedures agreed upon between the United States and the Soviet union. It is, however, appropriate for me to announce that Canada was invited to nominate a scientist to participate as one of the experts on the western side. It is therefore a pleasure for me to announce the appointment of Dr. O. M. Solandt, who for many years was chairman of the defence research board and is one of Canada's great scientists. Dr. Solandt is now vice chairman of the Canadian National Railways in charge of research, and has agreed to make himself available for this important and exacting assignment. Dr. Solandt's name has therefore been included in the list of western scientists contained in today's communication from the United States to the U.S.S.R.
I felt that this announcement should be made in the House of Commons simultaneously

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At one o'clock, Mr. Speaker,
I was pointing out that the Conservative party was a much different party from the Conservative party before the election as evidenced by the budget. One of the great problems remaining unsolved is the very widespread unemployment in our country. The budget is bare of any policy designed to put the unemployed back to work, and I think it is a shame and a disgrace to a nation such as our own that so much technical know-how and such a vast amount of plant and men should be idle at a time when many of our people are in great need.
The Minister of Finance brushed aside this aspect very quickly and lightly in his speech the other night, but he did not always brush the unemployment problem under the carpet in this way. In years gone by he was

The Budget-Mr. Argue very concerned about the question of Canadian unemployment, and on March 22 of 1955 he had this to say, as reported on page 2261 of Hansard:
When we entered this debate several weeks ago I am sure that all hon. members expected that the government would avail itself of this opportunity to make an announcement of whatever policy it proposed in order to grapple with a situation which is assuming emergent proportions.
He went on to say:
This session opened two and a half months ago with a statement by the government contained in the speech from the throne as follows:
"Some unemployment of a regional and seasonal nature is being experienced."
He said that the statement in the speech from the throne was a palpable and grotesque absurdity of understatement. That is what he said about the unemployment situation in March, 1955, at a time when there were 327,000 persons without jobs and seeking employment. However, in his budget speech, when he described the present unemployment situation as a fairly mild recession, there were no less than 556,000 persons at that time without jobs and seeking work. The minister, when he was a private member in 1955 and when unemployment was a great deal less, said something should have been done, but certainly this budget is bare with respect to action to alleviate the unemployment situation.
There are many things which should have been done in this budget; one thing certainly was to increase the income tax exemptions. The present exemptions of $1,000 for a single person and $2,000 for a married couple are completely inadequate. Because we feel there should be an increase in income tax exemptions, I wish to move a motion seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) as follows:
That the amendment be further amended by adding thereto the following words:
"This house further regrets that the government contemplates no action at this session to recognize the loss of purchasing power to the majority of Canadian citizens because of the lowered value of the dollar as related to consumer goods and prices, by amending the Income Tax Act so as to raise the amount of permissible income to single and married persons without taxation.

The official opposition was tried as the government of this country for 22 years and was found wanting, and was very rightly turned out of office on June 10 last, but the new government that has taken office since is no different. They took a short step forward when they were only a minority in this house, but they are now back to the

economic policies which resulted in their predecessors being turned out of office. We say to the people of this country at this time that there is only one movement that should be supported by people who are progressively minded, or liberally minded and that is the C.C.F. movement, and we look forward to the day when the people of this country will accept our policies. Before putting the amendment to the amendment, may I say a word about the amendment itself, which reads, in substance:
That this house regrets that the government in its budget proposals has failed to cope satisfactorily with the problems of the recession in spite of the largest peacetime deficit in Canadian history-
I accept the amendment to that point, but I raise for consideration the latter part of the amendment which seems to me to duplicate an amendment moved on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The latter part reads as follows:
an<i that it is moving towards greater trade restrictions at a time when other countries in the western world are moving in the opposite direction.
Now the amendment moved by the official opposition on the address in reply to the speech from the throne read:
We respectfully represent to Your Excellency that a high level of employment and prosperity in Canada requires a high and expanding level of international trade, and that this will be promoted more effectively by vigorous measures for the expansion of trade with all countries than by efforts to divert from one country to another.
It seems to me that the second half of each amendment is essentially on the same subject, and I wonder whether the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) would agree, in the absence of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), to the deletion of the second half of the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, with great respect I should like to call to your attention the fact that our earlier amendment dealt with the question of the expansion of trade as
The Budget-Amendment
opposed to the diversion of trade. This amendment deals not with one form of trade restriction, which might be diversion, but with trade restrictions generally, and puts those trade restrictions in the context of the general policies of other countries leading in the opposite direction. In other words, the amendment seeks to draw a contrast between the trade policy embodied in this budget and the policies which are being followed by other countries in the world, and I should have thought with great respect, Mr. Speaker, that this distinguishes it from the amendment we raised to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
perhaps you would wish something to be said from this side of the house on the question that has been raised. As I understand the rules of the house, it is that there may not be duplication of debate in the sense that when there has been a debate on a subject, that debate may not be revived during the session by the introduction of what is in substance the same question. It is not necessary that the second motion or amendment be in precisely identical terms; it is a question whether debate on the subject is, in essence, revived by the second measure, motion, amendment, or whatever it may be, which it is sought to introduce.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) has sought to distinguish the motion he introduced on May 13 from the second part of the amendment introduced this morning by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) by saying that they both relate to trade but that the earlier motion relates rather to the diversion of trade, thus seeking to contrast diversion of trade with expansion of trade, whereas the second half of this morning's amendment purports to condemn the government because it is said that there has been a movement toward greater trade restriction.
Looking at the matter, not in terms simply of the words but in terms of the substance, it is perhaps clear that there will be some duplication of debate. At the same time, I believe that it will be the desire of all hon. members that there should be the fullest opportunity for the discussion of trade policy during this debate. In response to previous requests I reviewed the position and policy of the government in relation to trade, with particular reference to our trade relations with the United States and the efforts we are
147S

The Budget-Mr. R. A. Bell making to expand trade within the commonwealth, and while it may well be that the amendment could be more happily worded to allow the fullest discussion on those points, I for one would not wish to see any undue limitation of the discussion of the trade questions and policies that are directly presented to the house by the budget. I may have my own opinion about how far this particular amendment strays away from those policies that were put before the house in the budget speech or which are raised directly or by implication in any of the budget resolutions. But, Mr. Speaker, I do think in this debate, as long as there is no trespass on the matters that were included in the earlier debate, it would be the wish of the house to have a full opportunity to discuss those questions of trade that were raised by the budget.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am prepared to accept the view as expressed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) with the reservation that he claims there is a distinction and perhaps I may try to find a distinction in the course of the debate. No one wants to proscribe a free-ranging debate of the kind of the budget debate and I accept the second part of this amendment as relating to the fiscal policy of the government related to trade and therefore opening the door for this kind of discussion.
May I now put the motion moved by way of amendment to the amendment. It is moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) and seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge):
That the amendment be further amended by adding thereto the following words:
This house further regrets that the government contemplates no action at this session to recognize the loss of purchasing power to the majority of Canadian citizens because of the lowered value of the dollar as related to consumer goods and prices, by amending the Income Tax Act so as to raise the amount of permissible income to single and married persons without taxation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house has heard two vigorous speeches from hon. gentlemen who take their roles as critics rather literally. As I listened to their rhetoric-indeed to their declamations-I was reminded of Disraeli's remark, "How much easier it is to be critical than to be correct". Such congratulations as I may extend to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) I must reserve first to congratulations upon the confidence his party has demonstrated in him, and properly so, in designating him for the important and onerous role of financial critic, and second upon the pleasant manner of his speaking in this house.
From the gallery of this chamber it has been my privilege to hear every financial

critic since the year 1927: Guthrie, Bennett, Ralston, Lawson, Hanson, Harris, and more recently the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), the latter I suppose being the veteran budget critic of all time. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River in taking this role has joined distinguished company and I extend my wishes to him in the words once used by the late Ernest Lapointe, "I wish him luck, but not too much".
I spoke of the onerous role of financial critic that now falls to the lot of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. Onerous and arduous that role will be for the hon. gentleman as long as the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) occupies the treasury benches as Minister of Finance. But what disappointed me in the speech of the new financial critic-and I must confess it immediately-was that he fell into the same error as his immediate predecessor, the former member for Coast-Capilano, in attempting to substitute angry scattered jibes and epithets for reasoned consecutive argument. May I say with respect that his was a speech conceived in angry frustration and delivered with a sense of bitter repression and electoral disappointment for these are the qualities which regrettably have characterized hon. gentlemen opposite since June 10 last.
Not yet have they reconciled themselves to the facts of political life. Not yet have they recovered from the complex they have of their divine right to rule. Perhaps it is because of that that in his speech and in the amendment which he moved the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has succeeded in getting on both sides of every issue, has succeeded in begging any question and has succeeded in blowing hot and cold on every problem. When he was speaking I set out to refresh my memory of the words of Samuel Butler, and these are they:
He was In logic a great critic
Profoundly skilled in analytic
He could distinguish and divide
A hair 'twixt south and southwest side.
On either which he would dispute,
Confute, change hand and still confute.
The speech of my friend the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) was merely a political stump speech, a warmed-over election hustings version. What serious contribution did the hon. gentleman make to this debate?

He appeared to be in favour of what he called quick economic stimulus by way of tax cuts, yet at other times he appeared to be in favour of tax maintenance. I thought I detected today that he was in favour of reduced expenditures but he was equally in favour of and called for higher payments. He was in favour of protection for Canadian industry and against all means of protecting Canadian industry. He was in favour of the expansion of trade within the commonwealth and against all means of achieving such expansion.
He was in favour of additional assistance to the provinces and to the municipalities yet rigidly adhered to the policies of the former government, rejected and discarded by the electorate, which prevented additional assistance to the provinces and the municipalities of this country. He was against dumping but in favour of the legislation which permits it. Never in such a short period of time did I ever hear one speaker gore himself on the horns of so many dilem-nas and I reflected, "Oh, Consistency, thou art a jewel!"
As I listened in incredulous fascination to the hon. gentleman I realized that the Liberal party continues as a house divided against itself. I realized how delicately and indecisively the hon. gentleman had to walk the tight rope in order to satisfy at the same time the Winnipeg Free Press and the party's eastern moguls.
