What about unemployment? I will tell you plenty about it and I will make it clear who is responsible for the present situation in unemployment before I am done if that is the issue the hon. gentleman wants to raise.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River laboured long and hard this morning to have this house and the country believe that the conditions of recession and unemployment have been a direct result of the economic and fiscal policies of this government. In fact, he would have us believe that it was contributed to by the failure of the government to present its budget earlier, perhaps last autumn, and by other alleged deficiencies which the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River described in terms rather more vivid than accurate. Let us examine these allegations. Let us put the situation in perspective. I suggest the best way to do this is to ask ourselves this question: What would have been the situation in Canada today if on June 10 last, by peradventure or misadventure, my hon. .friend's party had been re-elected?
I can tell you exactly what the situation would be. First, there would have been no budget or financial accounting of any kind at least until late this spring. This government did give a financial outline on December 6 last. Hon. members opposite have screamed for an autumn budget knowing full well that there would have been none if they had been in power. Actually all they were doing was administering another kick to the already well-bruised Walter Harris.
Second, there would have been no tax reduction as occurred last December. The Canadian people would have been deprived of the benefit of substantial tax cuts in personal income, corporation and excise taxes amounting to $178 million. These present advocates of tax reductions, of a tax holiday indeed, though that was not mentioned today, would have pursued the unrealistic policies laid down in the last Harris budget. I say, that that budget was as complete a miscalculation of the then existing economic position of this country as it was of the mood of the Canadian people.	[DOT]
Third, there would have been no increases in old age pensions beyond the Walter Harris-William Benidickson figure of $6 a month. There would have been no increases in disability pensions, in blind pensions, in war veterans allowances, no change in the Pension

These are but a few of the consequences which might have occurred without a change in the direction of the fiscal, monetary and commercial policies of the nation. It was a change of government, a change from the principles of the last Harris budget, with which the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River was so intimately connected, which saved this country from a major economic disaster. It was and is the realistic policies set forth in the speech from the throne and in the budget of last Tuesday night which will direct the paths of the Canadian people to greater and more ehallanging development, more challenging accomplishments and goals.
On Tuesday night the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River said, in an attempt to catch the headlines, that the budget was a sick budget. Did anybody in the house fail to realize on Tuesday night that all the sick faces were on the opposite side? More properly the hon. gentlemen ought to have called it a physician's budget, a budget designed to heal the many ills to which this government fell heir from its predecessor. He claimed that it was a wait and see budget, a slow motion budget. What nonsense! Never in the whole history of our country has there been a government which has attempted so much in such a short time. Yes, never has a government moved so rapidly its objectives to accomplish.
Then the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River used harsh words about the government respecting the projected deficit. He said this morning, 1 believe, that it was directly attributable to political commitments rather than to economic policy. What are

these commitments? Which of these commitments would he like us to abandon? What things has the government done involving financial outlays that he would seek to have undone? I think he should have told us that. I think hon. gentlemen opposite who speak later in the debate should tell us.
But, if I interpret my hon. friend correctly, and I think I do, if his policies were followed, certainly if his leader's policies had been followed, there could be no doubt that the deficit projected would have been at least $500 million more than what it is. How can he have it both ways? How can he manage, Janus-like, to face in both directions at the same time? Actually my hon. friend, I venture to suggest, resembles John Bunyan's great grandfather, "but a waterman, looking one way and rowing another".
No one denies that $648 million is an exceedingly sizeable surplus.

speechtext: Surplus?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Deficit, I am sorry. But it should cause dismay to no one. It represents 12.2 per cent of our total expenditure this year. There have been many times in our history, both under Liberal and Conservative governments, when the deficit has represented a very much higher percentage of expenditure.
To go back to 1909, if you will, to the great Liberal finance minister, W. S. Fielding, he had no concern over a deficit which represented 35 per cent of the total expenditure of that day. Nor had Mr. Dunning when his last budget before the 1930 election showed a deficit of 19 per cent of expenditure or when his first budget after the 1935 election showed a deficit of 14.6 per cent. Related to the gross national product, there have been many occasions when we have had larger deficits than that now projected. Nor are we alone in this country at this time with this particular problem. In the United States the best recent forecast indicated a deficit of between $11 billion and $13 billion, figures substantially higher on a per capita basis than that forecast in this budget.
But the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River reserved his harshest strictures for the calculation of the amount of the deficit. In effect he alleged a type of juggling of accounts to achieve a bookkeeping deficit smaller than the actual one. He bases this upon the winding up or liquidation of the defence equipment replacement account. On Tuesday night he went overboard in alleging incorrectly that provision had not been made in the deficit figure for $190 million for the old age security fund or $70 million for the hospital insurance scheme, but that
The Budget-Mr. R. A. Bell
he corrected today. He did try, however, to bring in the C.N.R. deficit and other nonbudgetary items although I am sure he is well aware from his experience that these have not been included in budgetary deficits on previous occasions.
But what of his strictures regarding the defence equipment replacement account? This account was nothing more than a bookkeeping kitty that the former government tucked away for convenient purposes to avoid parliamentary control of certain defence expenditures. At one time it was as high as $310 million. It is now $165 million. If the hon. gentleman suggests that the liquidation of the final balance of $165 million in this account distorts the budgetary position, then what does he say about the distortion when the former government reduced it by over $100 million? His argument, if it is logical and it is not, applies equally to the former government and he condemns his own colleagues by his ill-considered blasts in this respect.
I suggest to the house that there is no doubt that this account should have been eliminated several years ago. Indeed, at one time a former minister of finance ordered that it be liquidated within a period of three years. If his orders had been obeyed, what would my hon. friend have said? Would he then have charged the minister of finance with distortion, his own minister of finance with whom he served in such close relationship? Would he have charged him with distortion of the position? This government considered, in accordance with what is its universal policy, that parliamentary control of defence expenditures ought to be restored and that this bookkeeping device for circumventing parliament ought to be abandoned. It was, therefore, an honourable, honest course and was stated clearly, specifically and openly in the budget speech.
No one in the press gallery misunderstood, although my hon. friend may have done so. There was no concealment. The minister came right out in the open so that he who runs may read. I suggest this course was in refreshing contrast to the way in which previous ministers of finance were accustomed to tucking away $310 million in this account for the purpose of distorting the budgetary picture. What I want to emphasize is that this account has been a non-budgetary account used, however, by previous governments for budgetary purposes. This will be ended, and it will be liquidated as a nonbudgetary cash requirement. The cash position of the government is not changed, but the position of parliament and parliamentary control over the expenditure is greatly changed.

In a full year of office this government has taken no steps to give tariff or valuation protection to any industry except agriculture. Does my friend the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) object to that fact? With the exception of a group of miscellaneous tariff items in this budget, some of which involve small increases, but more of which involve duty reductions, and none of which have any major economic significance, all the tariff changes which have been made in this budget have been made on the recommendation of the tariff board. These tariff board reports, with one exception, were made at the request of the previous government.
When supporters of that former government say to us, as they have said today, that these tariff changes are restrictions on trade- and that is what the amendment says-what do they really mean? Are they saying that they would have declined to implement the reports of the tariff board on references which they themselves made? Are they admitting that these references were intended by them as purely dilatory tactics to get them over the embarrassment of dealing with these matters until after an election or what in fact does my friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River really mean?
The changes which have been made are changes negotiated in accordance with GATT and in full conformity with GATT. Wool fabrics are in a class by themselves. The desperate condition of the textile industry after years of Liberal neglect compelled some action, the full nature and import of which was clearly set forth in the budget address. My hon. friend would weep crocodile tears for the British exporters. To what extent will they suffer from the increase that has been put on in this budget? My hon. friend

said that it would cast a chill on the conference. I have greater faith in the British people and greater faith in the commonwealth than to believe, as he does, that this would cast a chill on what I believe may be the greatest movement forward in trade that we have had in many a year.
I want to say a word in respect to the prospective amendments to section 35 of the Custom Act. My personal view is that Canada made a grave mistake in 1948 when she amended the then provisions of that key valuation section of the Customs Act. Bit by bit, under pressure from many parts of Canada-and nobody knows this better than does the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River -the former government tried to restore some of the teeth in the former section. They did not succeed.
Mr. Speaker, I have no sympathy for any Canadian industry which cannot face reasonable and proper competition from imported goods. There is no use in having an industry in this country which has to be pampered and petted by excessively protective measures and which cannot face foreign competition on reasonable terms. But what this amendment is designed to do-as the Minister of Finance has outlined-is to eliminate foreign dumping. Surely there is no member of this house who wants Canadian industry, Canadian workmen, yes and Canadian agriculture, to be compelled to compete with foreign goods sold at less than their cost of production plus a reasonable amount for selling costs and profit. Yet, that is what my hon. friend the member for Kenora-Rainy River appeared to say this morning.
If preventing goods from entering Canada at less than their cost of production, thereby destroying the jobs of Canadian working men, is protection, then as far as I am concerned I am for that type of protection. As long as I have a vote in this house I will not vote to compel Canadian working men to compete with foreign dumped goods.
I have taken a substantial length of time on trade and tariff matters, but for that I do not apologize because the next few months will be critical and crucial ones for this nation's trading future. I believe it is the hope of all hon. members, wherever they sit in this house, that those who will assemble in Montreal on September 15 next for the great commonwealth trade and economic conference may have the wisdom and guidance to enable them to bring about a successful conclusion to that conference, one which will be advantageous to all nations.

Mr. Speaker, the great man has had a vision, a vision based on the promises made by the present government when it was sitting in opposition. However, when Conservatives are in power we have depression: For instance, under the Borden administration, we had the depression, unemployment and difficulties, and the same under the Bennett regime. On the other hand, under Liberal administrations we had unprecedented surpluses, unprecedented prosperity. Why were so many promises made? Why so much criticism? Why were they professing to be the champions of all classes when at present the government is protecting no particular class of society. Mr. Speaker, following so closely upon the brilliant speech of my colleague, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) and the equally dynamic speech of the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) which dealt with cut flowers, rat poison and the province of Quebec I am afraid the poor words which I will speak in the next few minutes are going to sound like a cap pistol being discharged following the sounding of a 21-gun salute. Nevertheless my words will be sincere.
As this is the first occasion I have had the honour to rise to speak in this house I would like to congratulate Mr. Speaker upon his re-election to the high post which he fills. To a new member of parliament it has been
The Budget-Mr. Stearns and is extremely comforting and encouraging to watch him perform his daily duties so wisely and in such a pleasant manner.
To you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, and to the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Rea) I wish to say I am both pleased and proud of the manner in which you maintain and preserve good order in the house.
As an English-speaking member from the province of Quebec I wish also to say how pleased I am at the recent appointment to ministerial rank of my two good friends, the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. O'Hurley) and the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche).
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for an Englishspeaking Canadian to have been chosen candidate in a constituency whose people are 75 per cent French-speaking. I can assure you that I was not chosen because I speak French well. You can readily realize that I speak this language with great difficulty. Therefore, I was not chosen on the strength of my ability as a speaker, I never was one, neither in French nor in English. I was chosen by the whole people of Compton-Frontenac which is a constituency of the eastern townships.
I appreciate French-speaking Canadians as much as I do English-speaking Canadians. I take advantage of this opportunity to thank all the electors who put their trust in me. We English-speaking Canadians of the province of Quebec are able to live in full harmony with our French-speaking fellow-citizens.
(Text):
About a week ago, I read an article in one of the Ottawa papers in which the writer referred to the quality of the speeches made during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The writer apparently took a dim view of those speeches. I think it is a pity that he did not wait until today because he would have had a better foundation for what he said than he had then. I enjoyed what I heard during that debate. The writer went on to say that he did not think newly elected members to parliament should confine their remarks to subjects concerning their own constituencies but that once they had come to Ottawa they should try to speak on subjects of interest to the whole country. I do not agree with that view because the only way this country can continue to be fairly governed is to have the problems and ideas of each of the 265 members presented to the house. The government can then sort them out, adopt those that are ready for adoption, discard those which are of no use and put the balance in a little pile on the

The Budget-Mr. Stearns shelf. As time overtakes these projects our friends of the C.C.F. group will see their ideas fulfilled.
I should like to say a few words about matters concerning my own constituency. I want to thank the government for the measures it passed during the short session of the last parliament which were of great benefit to the people of my constituency as well as to people all over Canada. I want to thank the government for extending the period of seasonal unemployment insurance benefits because I know for a fact that it did a tremendous amount of good in a small town in my constituency where the only industry had closed its doors forever.
I wish to thank the government for having started work on the Sherbrooke airport. I understand that the government intends to spend $4 million there during the next two years. This will provide a great number of jobs and in the future will result in interest on the part of a large number of industries in building factories close to the airport. Hon. members may ask why I am interested in the Sherbrooke airport. The reason is that all the land comprising the airport is in the county of Compton. My constituency is composed of the counties of Compton and Frontenac and it is significant that the two great races of our country live there side by side. The origin of the name "Compton" is lost in antiquity but it is believed to have been the name of a famous Englishman. As to the name "Frontenac", it is easily remembered as being the name of one of the great governors of New France.
The constituency consists for the greater part of small farms and some woodworking industries. The farmers cannot grow enough crops in the summer months to make a living so they turn to the woods in the winter time. When there is not sufficient work in the province of Quebec they go across the line to the states of Maine, New Hampshire or Vermont. If they work in Vermont all winter they are entitled upon their return home in the spring to draw unemployment insurance benefits in the province of Quebec because Vermont has a reciprocal agreement with Canada. Up to the present time neither the state of Maine nor the state of New Hampshire has been willing to enter into any such agreement. I suggest that the government keep on trying to convince the governors and legislative bodies of these two states to enter into reciprocal agreements so that our people working over there may be treated just as fairly as any United States citizen who happens to be working in the same camp.
Still on the subject of our farmers, I should very much like to see pulpwood brought


under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. In the first place, it might keep more of our farmers at home in the winter time if they had a winter crop which they knew they would be able to sell at a predetermined price. But most important is the improvement which would result in the quality of the pulpwood produced by the farmers if they had to follow standards and specifications laid down by the government in order to be protected by the floor price. The paper mills would certainly be prepared to pay a little more for the pulpwood if they could be sure that it was going to be usable when it got to the mill. At the present time almost anything is delivered to the paper mills of which there are three in the eastern townships. The wood is all mixed up and the companies buy it but they do not like it.
In the eastern townships we have 63 4-H clubs. Our 4-H clubs in the province of Quebec differ greatly from those in other parts of Canada and the United States where the emphasis is on dairy farming and crops. We cannot do that so well in the province of Quebec so our 4-H clubs are formed and maintained to teach the children forest conservation and to plant trees. We hope that as they grow up they will establish tree farms so that they will have a crop that they can sell in nearby markets during the winter. But it costs money in order to plant trees and protect them from disease and fire. Up to the present the farmers have not been able to afford to do very much about it. Some of the small forest industry companies give them trees and help them to get started. I know of one small company in the county of Frontenac that has been responsible for the planting already of over six million trees.
Having spoken about local problems, I should like to say a few words on the budget which has been brought down. I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for his courage in presenting a budget which is so realistic and in keeping with the difficult period from which we are just emerging. It is human nature to want to please as many people as possible and a giveaway program would have been much more agreeable to present. However, I have never felt that the Canadian people really expected to obtain any more than they did in the present budget. I say this because up to March 31 the Liberals were offering the people a very nice immediate tax cut of $400 million. If the voters had wanted it that way, they would have voted for the Liberals. The Liberals would have been re-elected and the present estimated deficit of $648 million would have reached over $1,000 million.

One of the great difficulties in connection with manufacturing goods today is the rapidity with which they are produced. If industry could only be geared to operate efficiently at about 80 per cent of its capacity, inventories would not tend to pile up so fast when there is a lull in demand. I am hoping that one lesson we will learn from this recession is to explore the possibility of providing full employment for the labour force we have now. I hope also that management and labour may work closer together so that we may never see the frightening day when our Canadian goods will be priced out of the markets of the world.
I do not believe that the small increase in the tariff on textiles will drive our friends away from our markets. I sincerely hope that the anti-dumping clause will put new life into this industry which has been depressed for so long. So far as lumber is concerned, I am happy that the recent difficulties of definition of planed lumber have been resolved. I am hoping to live to see the day when all tariffs and duties will have been removed from lumber which passes between the United States and this country. The right given to corporations to increase their donations for charitable purposes up to 10 per cent is a step in the right direction. It ought to help our hospitals and universities a great deal, but it might not be enough. If this proves to be the case, I hope our government will increase the allowance to 15 per cent of income or more. I hope the day never comes when our universities become state institutions because of a lack of support from corporations and private individuals.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish this parliament, so well endowed with youth, and I include Conservatives, Liberals and the eight youthful looking members of the C.C.F. who are not present at the moment, a most fruitful session to the benefit of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to express my views on the budget which was presented last Tuesday by paraphrasing a bit of a poem. "Something new, something blue", and I would add, "God, what a stew." As a matter of fact, it was something new. This was the first budget to be presented in two sessions of this parliament. The session last year was called to deal with matters generally, and at that time the minister did not dare bring down a budget. Oh, he brought in some changes, some cuts in taxes. I really believe he made a mistake because if he had introduced a budget last year with tax reductions amounting to $178 million and the increased pensions, it would have been presented to the people on the eve of the election in a very favourable light.
The Budget-Mr. Caron
However, the minister preferred not to present a budget. He introduced one this year which is really very blue. There is nothing in it to help the situation in which we find ourselves. Really, I would say it is a gloomy budget. I said that it was some kind of stew because the minister spoke a lot of words for over two hours, but nothing emerged to help the Canadian situation.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, during this budget debate, we are called upon of course to criticize the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for his presentation. Yet, knowing that there is nothing which is essentially good or essentially bad in this world, I take the liberty, at the outset of my remarks, to offer him my congratulations. I congratulate him for having been kind enough, for the first time in the history of Canada, when he presented his budget, to add a few sentences in French so as to show clearly that he recognized the bilingual character of Canada. It reminded me that I read the other night in the Sentinel an article entitled:	"Says bilingualism unrealistic,"
published by Rev. John Douglas, of Paisley Memorial United Church, and I quote:
(Text):
Like most of what is said in support of bilingualism in Canada it shows, to my mind, lack of logic and realism. No real argument is presented.
(Translation):

Let us ask ourselves why we should be bilingual, and what real benefits there are and we shall see that only in special cases is it worthwhile.
(Translation):
That is why I should like to congratulate the hon. minister for clearly demonstrating that he recognizes the bilingual character of our country. His French is very good and we accept it with pleasure. I would like to congratulate also-but it will be in his absence-the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) who, on two occasions

in Hull some time ago and in Montreal last Sunday-gave in good French some explanations about his opinion on obscene literature in Canada. Those two hon. ministers showed that articles such as the one to which I have just referred and which was printed in the Sentinel, are written by a minority of narrow-minded people who do not seem to have a true understanding of our country's problem. I think that this is a bad thing.
While I was a member of a delegation of the Canadian parliament to NATO, I found that among the fifteen countries represented there, most Europeans spoke perfectly in at

The Budget-Mr. Caron least two languages. The Belgians spoke from two to four languages; those from Great Britain spoke French and English to perfection. Unfortunately, English Canadians and Americans alone were unilingual, speaking only English. If, in the past, we had better understood the advantages of a twofold culture, there is no doubt that our representation abroad would have been in a more favourable position. Again I commend both hon. ministers.
(Text):
The other day I was reading Hansard for 1955, and I found these words spoken by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), and they appear in volume III, page 3392:
After the closest examination of the budget and of the minister's comments upon it, one can only conclude that this budget is the product of muddled thinking, confusion, indecision and fear on the part of the government to admit the existence of problems with which the taxpayers and the people of this country are all too familiar. It was therefore highly proper that The Economist in its issue of April 19, iri a letter from its Ottawa correspondent, should make this observation upon the budget:
"On the assumption that Canada needs some stimulus to get back to its proper rate of expansion after last year's modest setback, this financing of tax cuts out of deficit is easily defensible. The budget speech in fact made it perfectly clear that this was the intention. But the government refuses to say so explicitly. It has never admitted that anything was wrong with the Canadian economy that required artificial stimulus, and it will not do so now. It would rather do good by stealth. The result is to leave it without any logical defence of the plunge into deficit financing."
Could you find anything more realistic at the present time? I think we could have taken the whole speech of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) criticizing the budget of the Liberal party and it would be a speech that would be up to date after the budget we heard presented by the minister last Tuesday. As reported at page 3392 of Hansard he went on to say this:
It is true that in the house, constituted as this one is at present, the government wins the vote. But it is equally true that in relation to the kind of budget we are discussing here today the opposition wins the debate. But what of the people? The Canadian people from this budget will glean but little benefit but they will glean something of benefit from the debate in which the proposals of the government are examined.
It is perfectly true that the people of Canada will not get very much out of this budget. But after the discussion is over they will certainly have a clearer knowledge of the situation in which Canada is at the present time. One of the problems that the present government did not want to recognize and which it refused to admit last year was the problem of unemployment. When in October 1957 the Liberal party and the rest of the opposition were telling the ministers that it was dangerous to go on in the way we were

going, that unemployment was increasing every day and that they were not doing anything about it, the Prime Minister said at the time that the Liberals including our leader- and he especially mentioned our leader-were grossly exaggerating the situation, and this statement appeared in the Citizen of that day. It is true that unemployment has been recognized since that time but the government waited so long to recognize it that unemployment was given a chance to increase to a figure which the Canadian people had not been accustomed to since the crisis of 1930.
In the budget the minister admits-he admitted it the other night-that there was a slackening in the economy. I believe those are his words. In a speech made outside the house the Prime Minister said that in order to avoid recession and to create work he would not stop at any financial obstacle. But at the present time we have unemployment and it is still going on, and nothing is really being done to help the situation or to create a new economy so that everybody in this part of the year, the summer of 1958, will enjoy a share of work in this country. Instead of admitting the fact that unemployment exists; instead of admitting it clearly, as he stated in 1955 when he was blaming the Liberal party, the minister said the other night that there are more men at work in these months than there have been in any previous years. Nobody will refuse to admit that fact.
Certainly there are more men at work because the population has increased but the problem is that there are thousands and thousands of people not receiving anything from the unemployment department because their stamps are through, because they are not eligible for one reason or another. But those people are starving at the present time and the government is not doing anything to help them. I think of a doctor who is taking care of a sick person going into a hospital and for whom the only remedy he can find is to tell him that there are millions of millions of people on the street who are healthy and that he is one of the few in the hospital. Would such a remedy cure that person? That is what the Minister of Finance was doing in his budget last Tuesday. I come back to the opinions expressed in 1955 by the present Minister of Finance in criticizing the Liberal government. They are to be found in volume 3, page 3396 of Hansard. The minister said this:
The second problem which has been ignored by the government is the problem of unemployment.
That is what he said then.
This problem has been discussed at length in this session, or I would seek to go into it at greater length today. But let me content myself, in this limited time, with making this limited observation

on the subject, that the government throughout this session has observed a conspiracy of silence in regard to unemployment;-
This can be said for today.
-and it has carried that conspiracy of silence into the budget.
That can be said for today.
It is still running away from the problem of unemployment.
This can be said for the budget of today.
This budget does not meet, in fact it cannot even make the pretence of meeting or even assisting to meet, the problem of unemployment. The government is still running away from that problem; they hope to ignore it.
That is what we can say today; we can say what he said at the time when he was criticizing the Liberal government. If I may go a little further, on page 3396 in the same volume we find him reading a quotation of what Mr. St. Laurent had said outside the house. The quotation is as follows:
We have a country where there should be work for everybody and if we are not smart enough to organize the economy of the nation to provide work for everybody we are incompetent.
The present Minister of Finance said at the time:
And we say to the Prime Minister, "Out of thine own mouth hast thou condemned thyself, and not only thyself, but condemned thy colleagues as well".
If there is anything true it is this. If we transport those phrases pronounced by the Minister of Finance when he was on this side of the house in 1955, that is exactly the situation today. I think he was trying to prophesy then what would come about today if he were in power. He said this:
This is a problem that is national in scope. It is beyond local responsibility. What we want on the part of this government, and what we still look for, are employment measures, some constructive and some effective approach to meeting the deterioration m the economic condition and the unemployment situation in Canada today.
Is there really anything being done with respect to public works in order to help anybody? The Montreal Gazette of February 19, 1958, reported that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) announced on February 18 expenditures by government departments and agencies on works projects totalling $280 million during the first quarter of 1958 and $1,185 million for the full calendar year.
The other day we studied the estimates of the Department of Public Works, but what did we have in those estimates? They were pretty nearly all concerning things started by the Liberal government, in fact all the big things were commenced by that government. Where is this expenditure of $1,185 million? The government seems to think it
57071-3-95i
The Budget-Mr. Caron is doing a lot to help unemployment, but we cannot find any evidence of this.
We find instead a deficit which would be quite understandable if anything was being done to alleviate unemployment, but a deficit when nothing is being done along these lines is, in my opinion, due to maladministration of the affairs of the country.
I said in this house a few weeks ago that in the city of Hull 51 per cent of the unemployed were not receiving any unemployment benefits at all and the city itself has to accept responsibility in order to keep such people from starving. But, as the present minister said in 1955, this is not a problem for the local government, it is a problem for the federal government. Local authorities have no powers of taxation whereby they can obtain the money to help the unemployed. At the present time such people are being given a few dollars a week in order that they may have something to eat but they are not able to pay their rent and as a result may be thrown out on to the streets.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member state what tax he proposes might be used to take care of the situation?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am merely proposing that the government should stand by the promises made during the last election, when they said they would help the unemployed.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This they are not doing at the present time.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But what tax does the hon. member propose should take care of expenditures of this kind?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the problem of the government. When we are in trouble we do not mind a deficit provided such people are assisted, but when nothing is being done to help them that is a different matter. Our cities are in a very bad position; they cannot obtain the money to help them carry that burden. In the city of Hull, for example, expenses in respect of public assistance totalled $180,000 in 1953-54; in 1957-58, $480,000; and it is not fair for a city to have to spend such a sum. There is no sense in this situation-such expenditures are much too high for the municipalities and the government which promised it would help the municipalities has not yet done anything. Furthermore, they do not seem willing to do anything; they do not even try to do anything. All we can find in the budget are a few small reductions in the sales tax which will amount, as the minister said, to a total of $5 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The figure was $6 million for a full year.

The Budget-Mr. Caron Mr. Caron: Not for the municipalities. The minister said $5 million for the municipalities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh yes, that is right.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When we divide that $5 million among all the municipalities of the country each one will get a peanut.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They cannot take it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The municipalities have a heavy load to carry. We thought the Prime Minister would live up to his promises. The Montreal Gazette of February 8, 1958 reported that the Prime Minister on February 7, 1958 said he planned to call an informal federal-municipal conference in 1958 to discuss the financial plight of Canadian municipalities.
On February 26 the Montreal Star reported the Prime Minister as follows:
He also indicated prompt action on holding an "informal" meeting between the federal government and municipal representatives-he said it would occur after the election-to hear municipal views on their financial problems.
Such a meeting, he said, would allow the federal government to draw up proposals to present to the next federal-provincial conference for easing "excessive" municipal real estate taxes.
These are not my promises; they are the promises of the Prime Minister and his government. In the Ottawa Journal of February 26 the Prime Minister is reported as saying:
Mr. Diefenbaker announced that he proposed to call a federal-provincial-municipal conference In the near future. He recognized that the municipalities come under the jurisdiction of the provinces, but saw advantages of having them represented at an informal conference which would give them opportunity to put forward their own proposals and to explain their needs. Out of such a conference, he said, might come some plan to ease the "excessive" municipal tax burden on real estate.
Then there is a further translation I would like to quote from he Droit of February 26, 1958, as follows:
Mr. Diefenbaker stated that the government understands the difficult financial position of the municipalities of the country. "We shall see to granting them a reasonable share of taxes", he said, "so that they will be able to meet the new needs arising from their rapid growth."
According to the Prime Minister the question of division should be studied by the governments concerned, but his government is said to be ready with a plan for municipal aid in the light of such a study and the recommendations of the provincial governments. Those are the promises and the government is still making promises; but what do we get today? We get the same old promises. Nothing is being done for the 
municipalities who are asking for aid from the government. We need a source of employment and the government is able to provide that source right away. The municipalities have all kinds of projects ready and the only thing they lack is money. They are unable to get money on the market today at a fair price, and one thing this government could do is to lend the municipalities the money they need for their projects at an interest rate comparable to the one paid by the federal government on today's market. This would ease the difficulties of the municipalities.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who brought in the tight money policy and cut off the availability of money?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would refer the hon. member to the governor of the Bank of Canada. He might be able to give you a good answer to that question.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It would be better than yours.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member seems to believe what was said by the Minister of Finance, but let me tell him this: the Minister of Finance is often off the beam, and I showed that when I was showing what he said in 1955. He was speaking of tax reductions. Tax reductions last year amounted to $178 millions; this year in every department tax reductions amount to $26 million. And he seems to be happy with that, and the hon. member on my left seems to be happy with it too.
But let us look at what is being said all over the world. Governor Harriman speaking in New York with regard to the United States recession said there should be an emergency tax cut. He further said, and I quote his words:
In my opinion it would be reckless to do little, and sensible and safer to take strong measures in this period.
I point out that Governor Harriman is a man considered to be an expert in finance; much better than some of the hon. members I see on my left. Tax reform in the United States to encourage individual incentive and promote the nation's economic growth has also been proposed by the Rockefeller brothers fund. The recommendation was made by a panel of 17 leading economists, and they urged an immediate tax cut to help expand employment and overcome the current recession. The panel emphasized, too, that the anti-recession tax cuts should be consistent with the more important long-term goals of tax reform.
This is from the United States, but we can find something in Canada. I have here

the report of the general manager of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and I should like to place on record the following recommendation made by that association: With total taxation-federal, provincial and municipal-now 29.8 per cent of net national income as compared with 22.3 per cent in 1939, and with federal taxes representing almost three-quarters of total taxes, the association has urged that every effort should be made to reduce federal taxation, submitting, among other things, that if more money is left in the hands of individuals and corporations it will have a stimulating effect on business generally, and in particular, will make increased Canadian capital available for the much needed investment in our primary and secondary industries.
These are not men in politics; they are men in business, and they are looking after their businesses, and that is why they are pressing the present government to set up a tax system which will ensure that the money will flow to the people. With better purchasing power in the hands of the people, the factories will be able to start again and more of our people will be able to find employment.
How many people will benefit as a result of the government's tax concessions? Not many, I venture to think. With regard to the proposed assistance for education we must wait until the bill is presented before we see whether this is what we want it to be. However, we have the cut flower tax reduction, and this may prove an economy to the Conservative party when its members celebrate their anniversaries. But I am afraid this will be of limited benefit, because the carnations which are created so beautifully by nature have never been blue, they are always, red, pink or white.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about that pansy you are wearing? There is a lot of blue in that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My pansy has a lot of yellow in it, and I am sure some hon. members would be very proud to wear it on July 12.
The Minister of Finance spoke the other day about ways of getting money, about loans to cover part of the expenditure. He spoke about the sale of bonds in Canada and expressed the hope that everyone would participate in the buying of such bonds. There is one thing which every hon. member has received by mail, namely the plan which has been submitted since 1941 by Mr. Laflamme for what he calls premium bonds. This is a way to get people to buy these bonds, with low interest but with a possibility of a prize to make them attractive. Some people will say that this is a mere gamble. I do not know, but let us suppose it is. Who is not a gambler at heart? We have been born gamblers. Who among us has given the order to be born here or there? It is an accident to be born; it is a gamble we have to take. One man is
The Budget-Mr. Caron born in English-speaking Canada; another is born to be a French-speaking Canadian-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that Liberal fiscal policy?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It may not be that, but I will answer the hon. member a little further. Every time in life we have to make a choice, that choice is a gamble. I think the Minister of Finance should study this question of premium bonds very carefully, because such bonds would sell in great quantities in Canada and people would be glad to take a chance on winning $10,000 or $25,000 or $50,000 a month.
The government-the Conservative party- are keen to imitate everything that comes from Britain. They should recognize that this system has been accepted in Britain. I have here a copy of the London Times giving the numbers and the amounts which have been won by the drawings last month. There is a long list of them. And those bonds which are being sold in England are also being sold at the present time under this administration in Canada, and if it is legal to sell them in England and in Canada I think it should be legal for the government to sell them. Anything which would help the government of Canada to find the money to get out of the difficulties in which we now find ourselves should be accepted and tried. All I am asking the government to do at the present time is to study the question.
Experts on trade promotion have been telling the government that they have not been doing very much to help trade in Canada, and speaking of taxes the government is happy to say that on account of the recession they had a deficit of $648 million which will amount to over $1 billion before the year is over.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How do you know that?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But after the last war we had to change the economy of the country because industry had to change from war purposes to peace purposes. In the 42 months from 1945 to 1949 the Liberal government made reductions in taxes amounting to $1,292 million; in 1945, $300 million; in 1946, $266 million; in 1947, $265 million; in 1948, $92 million and in 1949, $369 million. This is the reason that right after the war we were not subjected to a period of recession such as we experienced last year and this year and during that period of 42 months the debt of the country was reduced by $1,625 million.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Overtaxation. Why didn't you cut taxes then?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Conservative government should not be proud of its record. During this period of hardship what we need in Canada-

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin a country with a small population of approximately 17 million that produces foodstuffs to support a population of over 40 million-is a firm policy that will develop markets for our products. What is the government doing to win markets for Canada? Nothing at all. The government criticizes the policies of the government of the United States and indulges in criticism of this and that, but is it really making an effort to sell Canadian products? Not at all. I admit the government held a conference at Mont Tremblant with the British government which brought in suggestions concerning free trade between the two countries. After this happened the government hastily closed the conference and sent the British delegates back home.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you for free trade or against it?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The government should institute a public relations policy that will win markets for Canadian goods in other countries. With regard to the import restrictions in other countries Mr. J. C. Whitelaw, Q.C., in the report of the general manager of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association stated:
Import quotas and exchange restrictions in commonwealth as well as other countries are limiting the export of Canadian manufactured goods. Some further relaxation in the United Kingdom import licensing arrangements were made in August 1957, while the token import scheme continues in effect in 1958 with very little change. The British West Indies liberalization plan for 1958 is unchanged. Certain commonwealth countries found it necessary in 1958 to further restrict their imports of manufactured goods, due to deficiencies in their balance of payments.
The Aciing Speaker (Mr. Rea): Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry myself.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to belatedly extend my congratulations to the Speaker on his election to that high office and commend him for the tact and skill which he has displayed in guiding the deliberations of this house. I extend the same complimentary words to yourself and to the Deputy Speaker. May I express the hope that the patient attitude you have demonstrated with respect to new members will continue and that the sands of your good nature will not run out at least until I have completed what I have to say.
I would also like to extend congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in respect of his first budget and to say that in presenting it he has in an honest and competent way faced realities and has been able to come to grips with the fiscal facts of life and at the same time has been able to maintain benefits which have been derived from tax deductions introduced at an earlier date,


to add something to them and also has been able to provide for the extensive public undertakings of this government. It has been a Herculean task and he should be given full credit for it. I would like in particular to comment on the proposal with regard to succession duties. This suggestion is most welcome and together with the companion measure permitting a tax-free gift up to $10,000 of a home or farm will remove inequities and injustices which have been apparent in the past.
I described the task of the Minister of Finance as a Herculean one and in so doing I had in mind that this government had to acquire some of the characteristics of Hercules in cleaning up after the previous administration by altering their unfortunate financial policies and doing what had to be done to remove the effects of such policies. I was thinking particularly of the task which was assigned to Hercules in cleaning out the Aegean stables for the first time in 100 years and I am sure the present Minister of Finance is thankful that he had only 23 years' accumulation to deal with.
I would now like to relate what was said in the conclusion of the budget presentation about the great destiny of this nation to observations I wish to make regarding a problem which affects the country generally and my constituency in particular, namely the question of the proposed construction of a railway to be built to the south shore of Great Slave lake.
The constituency which I represent is one of a tier of ridings lying at the northernmost extremity of the western provinces and occupying over one-third of the province of Alberta with an area of 80,000 square miles and containing a population of nearly 70,000 people. The people who live in the district constitute a reasonable cross section of Canada in the ethnic sense as here the two main streams of our population have joined and into the river which has resulted have been poured the smaller tributaries comprising the sturdy and fine people of every racial extraction who make up this country, all of us proud to be and to be called Canadians.
(Translation):
I am happy to know that the district which counts several thousand French-speaking voters supported me during the last election by awarding me 80 per cent of their votes. I hope that when I shall again ask for their support on another occasion, I shall be able to express myself in French, and I beg my hon. friends to pardon the errors I might commit when speaking in this language for the first time.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to require that all companies created by the parliament of Canada be managed by a majority of resident Canadian directors. The exception is where such a requirement already exists as in the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act and in part III of the Companies Act. As I say, there is an exception in the case of these acts because they already have this provision. There is also, I believe, a provision in the Bank Act passed at the last session of parliament whereby insurance companies by mutualization can retain their Canadian identity. Therefore at the present time companies having to do with financial affairs such as banks and insurance companies are able to retain their Canadian identity under an act of parliament.
For an understanding of the purpose and intent of the bill I should like to go back and establish the groundwork with regard to the present status of foreign investment in Canada and some of the conclusions which can be drawn from the amount of foreign investment. In doing so I wish to refer particularly to the Gordon report and to the report on Canada-United States economic relations by Messrs. Brecher and Reisman. In the late nineteenth century most foreign investments in Canada came from the United Kingdom and were mainly concentrated in railways, government bonds and the construction of basic utilities. In this regard foreign investment in Canada followed the pattern as it existed in the United States, a pattern which existed up to about the year 1914. However, in recent years foreign investment has mainly been in the form of equities, that is, in the form of investments participating in the growth of the country through investment in the petroleum industry, manufacturing industry and so on.


The extent of that investment is rather extraordinary. According to the report on Canada-United States economic relations, between 1900 and 1955 foreign, long-term capital invested rose from $1.2 billion to $13J billion. Actually that is a little bit out of date because the latest bureau of statistic figures as reported in the Toronto Telegram of June 16 indicate that the foreign stake in Canada's economic future has climbed to more than $17 billion, an increase of several billion dollars over the figure given in this report.
At present nearly four-fifths of all this foreign capital invested in Canada is held in the United States which is in strong contrast with the position at the end of world war I when the majority of foreign capital was held in the United Kingdom. At the beginning of 1955 non-residents controlled 54 per cent of the investment in Canadian manufacturing and 59 per cent of the total in mining, smelting and petroleum exploration and development. In fact, the holding in the petroleum industry alone would approach the 90 per cent mark. In a large number of very important Canadian industries, including oil, gas, nickle, aluminum, asbestos, iron ore, automobiles, electrical, rubber and chemicals, a relatively few enterprises owned and controlled mainly in the United States account for a very large share of the business enjoyed in those industries.
This is not to say that foreign investmenl in itself is not something that we are intensely anxious to have. In fact, our standard of living and the development of our country evolve around an adequate supply of capital from all countries throughout the world. But there are many questions which do come up and which should be considered in considering the problem and the longterm effects of this rather large foreign investment in our productive industries and our natural resources. It has been said that it is just a question of the economic immaturity of Canada and that in the course of time this condition will rectify itself in the same way it did in the United States. Actually this will not happen because, as I have pointed out, the bulk of the investment in the United States was in the form of underwriting government bonds whereas the investment in Canada is in the forms of equity stock.
Government bonds mature periodically and there is a chance then to repatriate them. Equity stock is something different. There is very little chance of repatriation of such stock unless a whole company is bought out in a company merger and the usual thing is that the smaller companies merge with large companies rather than vice versa. Therefore a very large proportion of foreign investment

in Canada involves direct ownership and control of productive enterprises.
In the past, with the growing maturity of the Canadian economy, a number of foreign corporations appear to have broadened the range of Canadian participation in their operations in a variety of ways because they found that the question as to how far foreign owned and controlled business enterprises should become integrated in the Canadian community was something which they should consider for self-interest reasons alone. As I say, many of these companies have moved in that direction and, to all intents and purposes, have become strictly Canadian enterprises. However, this report on Canada-United States economic relations goes on to point out the following:
With the increasing Canadian concern over the extent of foreign ownership and control, it is perhaps safe to predict that some acceleration of this process-
That is, greater Canadian participation.
-is likely to occur. On the other hand, there is no reason to believe that close integration will automatically become the universal pattern. While in many instances enlightened self-interest may stimulate further integration, in others the financial and operating advantages flowing from their present position may well continue to be the dominant consideration for non-resident enterprises.
This is a condition we must live with and it should be a cause of real concern. The extent of non-resident control has increased with the growth of Canadian industry and never in the economic history of any other nation as highly industrialized as Canada has there ever been such a large proportion of industry controlled by non-resident concerns.
That is roughly the situation as it stands today. It has been said that Canadian investment is an offsetting factor and that as other people invest in Canada so we in turn make investments in other countries. According to the report of the dominion bureau of statistics, as printed on June 16, Canada's investment abroad rose in the 1949-56 period to roughly $4.5 billion from $3.5 billion. However, as the bureau points out, a great deal of this so-called Canadian investment was really investment by Canadian companies which were really foreign-owned and which were returning money to parent corporations so that the parent corporation could make further investments in other areas of the world.
How did this situation come about? It is not the result merely of the fact that Canada has more than welcomed the investment of foreign capital here. This would not have been sufficient to attract the inflow of capital to this country of the magnitude we have had, nor would the availability of rich and plentiful resources and opportunities for growth
20, 1958
Company Directors' Qualifications have done so. I quote from page 385 of the Gordon commission report:
But the mere fact that Canada has been willing to borrow abroad and has always welcomed the investment of foreign capital here would not by itself have been enough to attract an inflow of capital to this country. Nor would the availability of rich and plentiful resources and opportunities for growth. Fortunately in addition the "investment climate" in Canada has been favourable. Canada has had a long tradition of freedom for the flow of capital and income across its borders. Canada has also had a long history of orderly and responsible government. Moreover, a hard-working people with a strong desire for material advancement, a skilled labour force, a well developed educational system, adequate transportation and other social-capital facilities, reasonably stable economic and social conditions and positive encouragement by all levels of government have all helped to make this country an attractive outlet for private foreign capital.
There are other and much more positive factors than those which have encouraged the people of the United States as well as Europeans to invest their capital in Canada. For instance, the United States economy has developed to the point where it is generating large amounts of savings. There are many people in the United States, including those responsible for managing large United States corporations, who are looking outside the borders of the United States for a suitable place to invest capital. Secondly, another motive for the investment of capital in Canada is to secure resources, that is resources which may be needed for future development of the company concerned, resources which may be falling off in the native country of that corporation.
Then the motive for direct investment by non-residents in Canadian secondary manufacturing industries has been to expand the parent companies' operations into the Canadian market in the most desirable way. There is the wish to take advantage of commonwealth preferences which such a company could secure through Canadian operation. In addition, there are taxation considerations, particularly in the United States where income tax concessions are designed to encourage people of the United States to explore for gas and oil, not only in the United States but other countries of the world as well. These concessions have given many United States citizens a natural incentive to come to Canada and explore here for oil and gas. The advantages of such investment to Canadians are equally clear. The profits from direct investments by foreign concerns have a direct influence on the rate of economic growth and industrial development and on the Canadian standard of living for Canadians.
The point about access to markets bears constant repetition and continued emphasis. Most of the output of many of Canada's basic
