Company Directors' Qualifications industries cannot be consumed at home and must be exported. In such circumstances the assured market which foreign parent companies can often provide to their Canadian subsidiaries may be imperative to offset the heavy risks which otherwise would be inherent in the large-scale capital investment which would otherwise be required to develop these industries. These benefits are very real and tangible. It is much more difficult to set down in precise terms what the dangers are. No nation has ever gone through the period of development through which we are going. No other nation has ever been in the same condition as we are in Canada in regard to the control of our resources and our manufacturing potential being largely outside of the country. It may be that much that has been said about foreign control has little, if any, validity and is simply an outgrowth of a rather youthful nationalism.
But on the other hand, there are many cases, many of which I know myself, where such control has not been entirely in the best interests of Canada. This concern has arisen because of the concentration of foreign ownership in certain industries, because of the fact that most of it is centred in one country, the United States, and because most of it is in the form of equities which, in the ordinary course of events, are never likely to be repatriated.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what would be the solution? I am not claiming that this bill is the solution. Before I conclude, I should like to quote the recommendations of the Gordon commission. Their recommendations were as follows:
(1)	wherever possible, such concerns should employ Canadians in senior management and technical positions, should retain Canadian engineering and other professional and service personnel, and should do their purchasing of supplies, material and equipment in this country;
(2)	they should publish their financial statements and make full disclosure of the results of their Canadian operations;
(3)	they should include on their boards of directors a number of independent Canadians and they should sell an appreciable interest in their equity stock to Canadians.
In so far as this bill is concerned, it states that the majority of the directors shall be resident Canadians. I checked with a very large firm which had business outside of Canada and they advised me that in their operations in Brazil the requirement they have to meet is that the majority of the directors shall be residents of that country. It may well be that the purpose of this bill could be equally well served if it said that these directors should be resident in the country rather than that the majority of directors should be Canadians. This is one of the reasons why I say I do not consider this


bill is the final and complete answer. However, the debate which the bill will provoke will help to resolve, in a slight way, some of the problems that we have in this regard by the contribution that it will make. By the contributions which are now being made by Senate committees which are at present studying United States-Canadian relations, by special committees such as those mentioned by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) which are being set up or have been set up to discuss United States-Canadian relations and by the work which is being done in that regard by the companies which are more conscious of the problems in our relationship. I say that is the way in which this condition, which I have been trying to point out can be to the detriment of Canada, can be resolved in a way that is mutually profitable for both countries. It is a question of education and it is a quesion of fair treatment to all concerned.
I should like to point out two or three conditions under which we are at present suffering. For instance, I have here a report from the Toronto Globe and Mail of April 15, 1958. The heading on this report or this news item is as follows:
Subsidiaries Hiring U.S. Engineers, Report Canadians Squeezed Out.
This is an interview with Lieutenant-Colonel T. M. Medland, executive director of the Association of Professional Engineers in Ontario who said as follows:
"We have been raising the devil over the installing of these natural gas pipelines. But we don't object to U.S. specialists being brought in provided they add Canadians to their staffs for training purposes."
He added: "But some companies with subsidiaries in Canada are attempting to hold their engineering staffs in the United States together by replacing Canadians in this country.
"The bigger companies are O.K. They are beginning to see the light and are interested in their senior staffs here being Canadians. We are more afraid of the smaller companies."
Actually the point that he is driving at is what happens in connection with a great many United States subsidiaries; and when I say "United States" I should use the word "foreign" because it applies to all foreign-controlled subsidiaries; but as I have pointed out previously, the bulk of our manufacturing, our engineering and our resource industries are under the control of the United States and therefore they are the people who bulk largest in this problem. But the problem does apply to all foreign countries. The difficulty has been that the Canadian operation has in many ways been considered as a branch plant extension of the parent company and as such is operated as a branch plant extension with all policy decision being made at the head office of the parent company.

The operating personnel in Canada are just that, namely operating personnel, and they have very little to do with such matters as export markets, the degree of Canadian content and other matters which would be of interest if it was not a wholly-owned subsidiary or even a partially-owned subsidiary which was for all purposes controlled in a foreign country.
You may think that that matter is not too important. But the fact has been that-and when I say "has been" I am not referring to all companies-in certain areas and with certain companies, for instance, purchasing policy has a definite United States bias with regard to the supply of material, machinery and equipment. The question of markets in many cases has been controlled from a parent company in the over-all interest of the company but sometimes not in the best interests of the Canadian company. There are examples of Canadian companies which have been precluded from participating in foreign markets which they could reach, in which they could sell and in which they have sold in previous years. By a policy decision made outside of this country they have been told that they are no longer free to ship into that export market.
Perhaps the problem which bears most heavily on our shoulders is that of senior personnel. Many subsidiaries' staffs-their managerial staff, their professional staff-are brought in from the United States and Canadian engineers and Canadian managers are not given a chance at promotion within that company. This is a much more general condition than hon. members of this house imagine it to be. I have here a letter from a young engineer who is a friend of mine. I will just quote one paragraph from it. He is referring to the fact that in the petroleum industry there is a general disinclination to hire Canadian engineers and there is an inclination to demand that key engineering work either be done in the United States or that personnel be brought over from the United States to do this work in Canada. He says as follows:
The state of affairs I speak about I realize is probably most noticeable on project work connected with the oil and gas industry but I suspect that the same thing holds for other parts of the economy as well. I am disturbed constantly by the number of surveys and investigations done by "a firm of American consultants". I was more disturbed recently while on a job hunting tour in Alberta to hear in the office of one American engineering firm in Calgary that Canadians couldn't be hired for work in Canada under present conditions when the company had plenty of Americans on its payroll trying to keep busy.
For those people who are from Calgary I might say that this firm said they had to make sure that their people in Denver were
Company Directors' Qualifications taken care of first. That is not an isolated case. I know of at least half a dozen. I am referring to highly specialized, highly trained technical personnel, graduate engineers, who could do the job but who will not be allowed to do so. This is along the same line of thought as that expressed in this newspaper comment that I read out a few minutes ago.
I was interested in putting a question on the order paper with regard to the value of automatic transmission assemblies and parts imported from the United States by the automobile industry. I found out that the Department of Trade and Commerce just could not give me that information. Then I asked for the duty rate and the answer is as follows:
Complete automatic transmissions for use in the assembly of motor cars are ruled to be of a class or kind not made in Canada and are admissible under tariff item 438n free of duty when imported from the United States.
Then I asked with regard to parts for automatic transmissions and I was told that since they were not made in Canada they came in duty free also.
I also recall many years in the automobile industry when the empire content clause reacted in favour of increasing the Canadian content in automobiles manufactured in Canada so that the automobile companies could participate in markets which were closed to them if they exported from the United States and which they could only enter from Canada. Their export markets reached from Canada are not so important to them now. Branch plants have been set up in Australia, Malaya and so on. So the Canadian content part is not too important, but there is another point I would like to raise and that is that approximately $10 million to $15 million worth of automatic transmissions are brought into this country. These products alone would, if made in Canada, provide employment for at least 300 men, and I would suspect the figure might run as high as 500.
The tooling problems are not great, and neither is the problem of capital investment. However, it is to the advantage of the automobile company to concentrate the production of automatic transmissions; in fact, in one company of which I know production is confined to one plant in the United States. These components are shipped into Canada and we will never institute an increasing Canadian content in the automobile industry unless the industry has some incentive to build up that content. If they were given such an incentive I suspect that there would be many more jobs opening up in Windsor and Oshawa. It is certainly not in the Canadian interest that this condition should be allowed to continue. I can assure hon. members that such items as automatic transmissions can be

Company Directors' Qualifications manufactured in Canada as cheaply as in the United States. In fact, as much automobile manufacturing is done in terms of labour hours and less time is used-if you ignore tooling costs-than is the case in the United States. I have also known of cases where United States engineers come up to study Canadian production methods, for example, in the Fisher body corporation, because those methods were more advanced than the ones practised in the United States.
I see my time is drawing to a close, but I would not wish to leave the impression that it is only United States firms who are not hiring Canadian personnel, because I notice in the Gazette that the Boyal Bank in Place Ville Marie has employed the services of architects and planners from the United States. In fact, if you read down the list, the first half dozen categories of architects, mechanical and structural engineers, indicate that most of this work is being done by New York organizations.
I believe, furthermore, that the Queen Elizabeth hotel was pretty nearly completely designed in New York. We are a nation which is apparently continually saying, "We do not have the know-how, the savvy, we lack the trained engineers and technical personnel." This is not so. We can tackle any job, and it is only in very few specialized fields that we do need outside help. My contention is that if somehow, through education, through bills such as this, or through modifications to such bills, we could create the general atmosphere in this country which would allow enterprises to make the greatest capital gain they can and to obtain the greatest share of the markets they can, generally to operate as a part of the Canadian community and industrial life, and indeed to pay their proper share of charitable contributions, this would be a great step in the right direction. I raise the last point because I understand that it is not possible for many of the operating heads of companies in this country to make a contribution to welfare or whatever the cause may be without first obtaining permission from their United States head office.
The whole intention of this bill is to create a condition, if not on the operative level, at least on the policy-making level between the operating heads of the Canadian and the parent companies, so that as the years go by the Canadian company will gradually increase its proportion of Canadian engineers, Canadian salesmen and indeed achieve a completely Canadian personnel, all working to the best of their abilities to make the Canadian operation a profitable one. These investments have come into our country and

have helped to develop Canada and the Canadian operation should try to produce as much as it can and to sell in as many markets of the world as it can in free and open competition, if necessary with its own parent company, and in competition with foreign companies.
The purpose of this bill is not to try to dictate to anyone or to drive away capital but, on the contrary, to set up a suitable atmosphere of a continuing nature which will be of benefit not only to the Canadian people but to the organizations who have invested -it is true for the sake of profit-in our country. We hope to provide a general climate in economic and industrial operations in Canada which will be of benefit to everyone.

subtopic: BOARDS OF FEDERAL COMPANIES TO HAVE MAJORITY OF CANADIANS
speechtext:
I would like to assure the hon. member who has just taken his seat that our party supports his bill on second reading, which is the stage where principle is involved. We hope that the bill will be thereafter sent to a committee where it may be examined much more closely because, as the hon. member himself pointed out, there are many factors which should receive further consideration. We trust there will be an opportunity for a vote on this bill before six o'clock, although the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) probably has other intentions.
I wonder whether in introducing the bill the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome) considered the fact that so many companies in Canada, especially those in the resources field, are not set up under the Companies Act or under letters patent from this parliament but come solely within provincial jurisdiction. As a matter of fact, I understand one of their main reasons for organizing on a national basis is because the federal service is better than that offered by some of the provinces. The fact remains that this bill could drive companies to let go their organization under a federal basis and concentrate on an exclusively provincial operation. I raise this point because I know that many of the pulp and paper companies in my own area operate entirely within the province of Ontario. This is a consideration which I think should be taken into account.
I wish the hon. member had made some further investigation of the files in the office of the Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche) with respect to the situation as to subsidiaries and as to whether there is any indication from the addresses of the directors of certain companies of how many such directors do live in Canada at the present time.
The intent behind the bill seems to me to be identified with the party of the hon. member. One usually thinks of a bill brought

in by a private member as being something which is particularly his own interest, but in this case, bearing in mind speeches during the last two election campaigns, there seems to be an absorbing fear on the part of the hon. member's party with respect to United States domination of the Canadian economy.
I can only say that I wish a few more of the private members on the government side had been similarly inclined because we would especially welcome a bill which would require the subsidiaries of United States corporations to publish an annual report showing the relationship of the Canadian subsidiary to the total operation of the concern. We believe this aspect of the matter is perhaps even more important than the requirement so far as the directors are concerned.
Another point that perhaps we could welcome in relation to this bill is the whole question of giving Canadians the chance to share in the equity possibilities of Canadian subsidiaries without having to go into the parent company for stock purchases, and we would certainly welcome it if the hon. member who introduced the bill could develop the tone even a little more, perhaps in the party caucus, and perhaps a few of the younger members could assist him in taking the initiative with regard to these matters which are so closely related.
One of the difficulties, it seems to me, in principle about this question of directorships is the corporate structure. I think it has been very noticeable. Any of you who have been reading texts in the development of corporate structure will realize that more and more control is going out of the grasp of the shareholders, or directors elected by shareholders, and entering the grasp of management itself. Furthermore, we have had a tremendous development in the last decade of two other factors which make the position of a director much less important and so gives the purpose of this bill perhaps more meaning. I am thinking of a giant holding company which needs to purchase perhaps only a minority part of the stock of a company before it can control it and set up its own dummies. That is another question which could be considered in the committee, whether these directors would be any more than dummies. I know in particular of a mining operation in the area from which I come where there are a number of Canadian directors but where the effective control, as everyone realizes, is not in the head office in Canada but down in the United States.
I am reminded of another story-I hope it is apocryphal-in connection with one of the companies laying the trans-Canada pipe
Company Directors' Qualifications line. Apparently they were having difficulty in getting past the Department of Citizenship and Immigration in getting some Americans in to work, so they took these chaps who were waiting down south of the border and who they felt were needed badly, and they created them vice-presidents of the company. I understand these men are working, one as a truck driver and one in charge of a parts store, and at the same time they are vice-presidents of this construction company, and that is an example of how a dummies set-up can come in, no matter how well intentioned the legislation.
One of the other tremendous developments I referred to earlier and that I have not touched on in detail yet, is the development of these investment portfolios by such organizations as Investors Mutual and Investors Syndicate. More and more, so much of the equity control seems to be superficially getting into the hands of these big portfolio groups and companies that they are in a position to nominate directors and in many ways almost control the policies of the corporation. I was just wondering, and it seems a very good question, how is this development-and it seems to be going on every year; in the Financial Post in their annual review you can see how these portfolios are getting larger and larger, and so the question comes to mind-eventually going to be applied. Are these portfolio-holding mutual companies to continue to keep hands off appointing directors and actually taking an interest in management, or is there finally going to come a switch and will they begin to operate more like a holding company. This question affects the question of selecting Canadian directors and the general problem, of course, seems to me that we have been told often enough by supporters of free enterprise in this house that capital is international and knows no bounds, and we cannot consider very seriously whether Canadian directors of United States owned subsidiaries can do an effective job.
This sounds very much like a general criticism of the bill, but it is only intended to be some suggestions to lead us on after second reading to a study of the bill in committee. We think that would be extremely worth while.
I do not want to close without saying some good things about some of the United States subsidiaries we have in Canada. I realize, for example, from my own particular training of librarianship that we would be nowhere in Canada but for funds supplied by a United States corporation, the Carnegie Foundation, and I think also of the work that has been

Company Directors' Qualifications done by other large United States corporations. We have got to temper our criticism to a certain extent with regard to the way they operate.
We have in our area two United States subsidiaries, the Marathon Corporation and Kimberley Clark, that in many ways have set the pace and the whole standard not only for the communities they have developed but also for the advanced forestry outlook they have. And when I consider what they do compared with, for example, a Canadian corporation such as Abitibi which has largely Canadian directors, I begin to see that there has been a certain guided benevolence on the part of some United States corporations, and that this bill might cause such organizations difficulty.
Then again, Marathon Corporation only recently became in the United States a subsidiary of a much bigger organization, the American Can, and I do know that the community of Marathon and those engaged in the home operations there stewed and worried for a few months because they knew that control was vested in the United States but they had come to recognize that the control was benevolent and very often in their best interests. Now it has been removed by another of these gigantic shuffles in the corporation market, and perhaps if we had a requirement such as the hon. member suggested in this bill we would not have this kind of worry.
I certainly think the point the hon. member made with regard to corporate contributions by United States subsidiaries to our Canadian educational institutions is a very important one and it would not be right to single out any particular United States subsidiary that is giving a great deal or others that have given nothing, but this is an important point. It seems clear that if one had Canadian directors with a Canadian background and education they would be much more likely to call to the attention of the management of the corporation the need for helping Canadian institutions.
That completes the remarks I want to make. I would just like to close by congratulating the hon. member again on his initiative.

subtopic: BOARDS OF FEDERAL COMPANIES TO HAVE MAJORITY OF CANADIANS
speechtext:
Before the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) spoke I had some misgivings about this bill. I have considerably more now, and in view of the well known and long standing love of private enterprise by that particular group my suspicions are naturally aroused by the sentiments he has expressed and by the congratulations he has extended to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome).

I should just like to say to him that the principles or objectives or intentions that he has in mind are indeed good if taken in proper doses but, as he says on his own admission, in effect the establishment of a majority of directors would not in itself cure the problem about which he spoke for some 40 minutes. It therefore seems unnecessary to make any comment on the bill as such because of its apparent weaknesses; first, that the aim he wishes to achieve could be completely defeated by provincial corporations or by establishing dummy directors, which makes it unnecessary to comment on the bill any further.
But he did raise one or two other interesting points with which I wish to deal, not in defence of foreign investment or United States citizens or United States companies but purely to set the record straight. In his remarks the hon. member made repeated reference to Canada's No. 1 industry, the petroleum and natural gas industry.
In dealing with the points raised by the hon. member the first comment I would make is this. We recognize perhaps as much as anyone the need for capital investment. We know that the capital requirements of Canada involving an investment of some $8 billion exceeds our ability in savings by a considerable degree. We also appreciate that we have vast areas of undeveloped sections of Canada and in western Canada in particular we have vast areas of undeveloped resources. It therefore becomes essential that if we are to enjoy the prosperity we have experienced these past years we must continue to develop these resources-yes, in the interests of Canadians first-and we can only do this, I suggest, with the aid of foreign capital.
The hon. member who introduced the bill said it was not designed to discourage foreign capital. I submit that the moment this bill was placed on the order paper it did exactly that.

speechtext:
You cannot say to anyone whether he be American, Belgian or Chinese that you are inviting capital from his country to Canada with strings attached to the invitation. It is tantamount to saying, "It is all right to send your money but do not come yourself." The hon. member for Port Arthur suggested that there are several ways of being absolutely certain that the rights of Canadians are protected and he itemized them. They are also contained in the report of the Gordon commission and have been enunciated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on several occasions. They were also set out in the brief presented to the Gordon commission by the Canadian

Manufacturers' Association. As they have already been dealt with I shall only say this in referring to them. Protection of the rights of Canadians in participating in the equity of these companies can be safeguarded by ensuring that Canadians have the right to participate in their management, by ensuring that these companies will carry out the development of research in the industries concerned, by ensuring that these companies will contribute to various philanthropic societies and also by ensuring that these companies will in themselves be good companies. I believe that to a substantial degree the United States parent and subsidiary companies operating in Canada have followed this pattern although of course there are exceptions.
With a recession today in the United States it is quite likely that a number of citizens of that country will enter Canada to establish themselves in Canadian industry. I have no facts or figures in this respect but it is something that conceivably could happen. We in the petroleum industry recognize that and the industry itself-not government-are taking every precaution by informing these companies that if they hope to retain their position here under the same favourable circumstances they have enjoyed in past years it is good common sense to be absolutely certain that they are first of all good Canadian citizens operating as good citizens should.
I wish to make one point clear with respect to the development of resources-and petroleum and natural gas are perhaps as good an example as any-and it is that large expenditures will be necessary to ensure continued development. It is estimated we are going to require to expend about $25 billion in order to develop the petroleum and natural gas industry in the next 20 years. It is obvious that we have two choices in this regard. The first is to call upon our own savings which I have suggested are not great enough to meet the demand and the second is that we merely delay the day when these resources are going to be utilized. Let us keep in mind that in developing the resources of our country we will be providing literally thousands of jobs for Canadians and millions of dollars in consumer goods in putting these products into competitive markets for the use, first of all, of Canadians.
I suggest it is not necessary to become emotional in judging the advantages of foreign investment. I point out that this bill will do nothing to encourage the free flow of the
Company Directors' Qualifications required capital to our country. For some years we had no opportunity and little hope of obtaining capital from eastern sections of Canada with which to develop the resources of western Canada. It was many years before Bay street was prepared to invest capital in the development of natural resources in Alberta and consequently the province accepted foreign capital from the United States in substantial volume.
I wish to raise one other point before concluding because I notice it is almost six o'clock. I wish to stress the necessity of maintaining proper provincial legislation to ensure adequate control by Canadians of our resources. This legislation is already in effect in the provinces which illustrates that foreign investment does not mean control of Canadian industry itself. We have all the provisions we require to protect the rights of our citizens. I am quite certain that the law makers in Canada, both provincial and federal, will conscientiously endeavour to ensure that Canadian rights are adequately protected.
I suggest that the intention of this bill is good in that the hon. member was motivated by a desire to ensure the protection of the rights of Canadians through the application of the five or six safeguards listed in the report of the Gordon commission but I point out that the bill will do little else but discourage the foreign capital which we certainly require at this stage in the history of the development of Canada's natural resources.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I presume we will proceed with the debate on the budget on Monday and continue it throughout the week, as was announced last night?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is the intention, Mr. Speaker. It has been agreed among the parties that private members' day which normally falls on Monday will be postponed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the house give unanimous consent that the business on Monday will be a continuation of the budget debate notwithstanding the provisions of standing order 15 (3) which would otherwise make it private members' day?
Agreed.

Questions
The following answers, deposited with the Clerk of the house, are printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

subtopic: POSTAL SERVICE, ROUTE 501, OTTAWA
POSTAL SERVICE, ROUTE 501, OTTAWA
speechtext:
1.	Is delivery of mall for boxholders served by route 501, Ottawa, made by department personnel or by contract?
2.	If by contract, what is the name of the contractor?
3.	Were tenders called for this contract?
4.	If not, for what reason?
5.	What is the price paid for this service?
Answer by: Hon. W. M. Hamilton (Postmaster
General):
1 and 2. Service performed under temporary arrangement with Rod Service (Ottawa) Limited.
3.	No.
4.	Due to the probability of considerable changes in the number of patrons to be served, it was not considered advisable to invite tenders for a regular contract until the situation has become more stabilized.
5.	$2.50 per hour for truck and driver.

subtopic: SPECIAL DELIVERY POSTAL SERVICE, OTTAWA
SPECIAL DELIVERY POSTAL SERVICE, OTTAWA
speechtext:
1.	Are special delivery letters in Ottawa delivered by a contractor or by post office personnel?
2.	If by contract, (a) who is the contractor; (b) what is the price paid for this service?
3.	Were tenders called? If not, for what reason?
Answer by: Hon. W. M. Hamilton (Postmaster
General):
1.	Special delivery letters are delivered in Ottawa by a contractor operating on a temporary basis, except for a limited number of items which can be delivered more expeditiously by letter carriers.
2.	(a) Rod Service (Ottawa) Ltd.; (b) 20 cents per item, plus $45 per month for each of three vehicles. Payment at pro rata is made for any additional vehicles required.
3.	No. It is not the practice to advertise special delivery services. Experience has proved that more efficient and economical arrangements can be made by utilizing the services of regular contractors holding mail contracts in the same areas.
